subject: Mathematics
question_english: A prayer hall must have a carpet area of 300 m², with length one metre more than twice its breadth. Form the equation and find the dimensions.
question_hinglish: Ek prayer hall ka carpet area 300 m² hona chahiye, aur lambai chaudai ke do gune se ek metre zyada. Equation banao aur maap nikaalo.
answer_english:
Breadth = x m, length = (2x + 1) m.
x(2x + 1) = 300 → 2x² + x − 300 = 0.
Split the middle term: 2x² − 24x + 25x − 300 = 0 → 2x(x − 12) + 25(x − 12) = 0 → (x − 12)(2x + 25) = 0.
x = 12 or x = −12.5; breadth cannot be negative, so x = 12.
Breadth = 12 m, length = 25 m. Jaanch: 12 × 25 = 300.

question_english: Check whether these are quadratic equations: (i) (x − 2)² + 1 = 2x − 3 (ii) x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2)(x − 2) (iii) x(2x + 3) = x² + 1 (iv) (x + 2)³ = x³ − 4. What is the lesson?
question_hinglish: Jaancho ki ye quadratic equations hain ya nahi: (i) (x − 2)² + 1 = 2x − 3 (ii) x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2)(x − 2) (iii) x(2x + 3) = x² + 1 (iv) (x + 2)³ = x³ − 4. Isse kya seekh milti hai?
answer_english:
(i) x² − 4x + 5 = 2x − 3 → x² − 6x + 8 = 0: quadratic.
(ii) x² + x + 8 = x² − 4 → x + 12 = 0: NOT quadratic (the x² terms cancel).
(iii) 2x² + 3x = x² + 1 → x² + 3x − 1 = 0: quadratic.
(iv) x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8 = x³ − 4 → 6x² + 12x + 12 = 0 → x² + 2x + 2 = 0: quadratic (the x³ terms cancel).
Lesson: (ii) looks quadratic but is not, and (iv) looks cubic but is quadratic. Always simplify before deciding.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Represent as quadratic equations: (i) a rectangular plot of area 528 m² with length one more than twice its breadth; (ii) two consecutive positive integers with product 306; (iii) Rohan's mother is 26 years older and the product of their ages 3 years from now is 360; (iv) a train covers 480 km, and 8 km/h less speed would take 3 hours more.
question_hinglish: Quadratic equations ke roop mein likho: (i) 528 m² ka rectangular plot jiski lambai chaudai ke do gune se ek zyada hai; (ii) do lagaataar positive integers jinka guna 306 hai; (iii) Rohan ki maa usse 26 saal badi hai aur 3 saal baad unki umar ka guna 360 hoga; (iv) train 480 km chalti hai, aur 8 km/h kam speed pe 3 ghante zyada lagte.
answer_hinglish:
Variable maankar equation banao:
(i) Chaudai x: x(2x + 1) = 528 → 2x² + x − 528 = 0.
(ii) Integers x, x + 1: x(x + 1) = 306 → x² + x − 306 = 0.
(iii) Rohan ki umar x: (x + 3)(x + 29) = 360 → x² + 32x − 273 = 0.
(iv) Speed x km/h: 480/(x − 8) − 480/x = 3 → 3840 = 3x(x − 8) → x² − 8x − 1280 = 0.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: What is a root of a quadratic equation? How many roots can it have?
question_hinglish: Quadratic equation ka root kya hota hai? Uske kitne roots ho sakte hain?
answer_english:
A real number α is a root of ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) if aα² + bα + c = 0. We also say x = α is a solution, or α satisfies the equation.
The zeroes of the polynomial ax² + bx + c and the roots of the equation ax² + bx + c = 0 are the same.
Since a quadratic polynomial has at most two zeroes, a quadratic equation has at most two roots.
Example: 1 is a root of 2x² − 3x + 1 = 0 because 2(1)² − 3(1) + 1 = 0.

ncert_context: Example 3: Find the roots of the equation 2x² – 5x + 3 = 0, by factorisation. Let us first split the middle term – 5x as –2x –3x [because (–2x) × (–3x) = 6x² = (2x²) × 3]. So, 2x² – 5x + 3 = (2x – 3)(x – 1). So, x = 3/2 and x = 1 are the solutions. Example 4: Find the roots of the quadratic equation 6x² – x – 2 = 0. 6x² + 3x – 4x – 2 = (3x – 2)(2x + 1). Therefore, the roots are 2/3 and –1/2. Example 5: Find the roots of the quadratic equation 3x² – 2√6x + 2 = 0. 3x² – √6x – √6x + 2 = (√3x – √2)(√3x – √2). So, this root is repeated twice, one for each repeated factor. Therefore, the roots are √(2/3), √(2/3).

question_english: (a) John and Jivanti together have 45 marbles; after each loses 5, the product of what they have is 124. How many did each have? (b) A cottage industry's cost per toy is 55 minus the number of toys made; one day the total cost was ₹750. How many toys were made?
question_hinglish: (a) John aur Jivanti ke paas milaakar 45 kanche hain; dono 5-5 kho dete hain to bache hue kanchon ka guna 124 hai. Har ek ke paas kitne the? (b) Ek cottage industry mein ek khilone ki laagat 55 minus banaye gaye khilone hai; ek din kul laagat ₹750 thi. Kitne khilone bane?
answer_english:
(a) John x, Jivanti 45 − x: (x − 5)(40 − x) = 124 → x² − 45x + 324 = 0 → (x − 36)(x − 9) = 0 → x = 36 or 9.
So one had 36 and the other 9 marbles. Jaanch: 31 × 4 = 124.
(b) x toys: x(55 − x) = 750 → x² − 55x + 750 = 0 → (x − 25)(x − 30) = 0 → x = 25 or 30 toys.
Jaanch: 25 × 30 = 750.

question_english: (a) Find two numbers whose sum is 27 and product 182. (b) Find two consecutive positive integers the sum of whose squares is 365.
question_hinglish: (a) Do numbers nikaalo jinka jod 27 aur guna 182 hai. (b) Do lagaataar positive integers nikaalo jinke vargon ka jod 365 hai.
answer_english:
(a) Numbers x and 27 − x: x(27 − x) = 182 → x² − 27x + 182 = 0 → (x − 13)(x − 14) = 0. The numbers are 13 and 14.
(b) Integers x, x + 1: x² + (x + 1)² = 365 → 2x² + 2x − 364 = 0 → x² + x − 182 = 0 → (x + 14)(x − 13) = 0 → x = 13 (positive).
The integers are 13 and 14. Jaanch: 169 + 196 = 365.

6 articles at ₹15 each.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: State the quadratic formula. What is the discriminant and how does it decide the nature of roots?
question_hinglish: Quadratic formula batao. Discriminant kya hai aur ye roots ka nature kaise tay karta hai?
answer_english:
The roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 are x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, provided b² − 4ac ≥ 0.
b² − 4ac is called the discriminant, because it determines whether the equation has real roots.
(i) b² − 4ac > 0: two distinct real roots, (−b + √(b² − 4ac))/2a and (−b − √(b² − 4ac))/2a.
(ii) b² − 4ac = 0: two equal real roots, both −b/2a.
(iii) b² − 4ac < 0: no real roots, since no real number has a negative square.
answer_hinglish:
ax² + bx + c = 0 ke roots x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a hain, agar b² − 4ac ≥ 0 ho.
b² − 4ac ko discriminant kehte hain, kyunki ye tay karta hai ki real roots hain ya nahi.

question_english: A pole is to be erected on the boundary of a circular park of diameter 13 m so that the difference of its distances from two diametrically opposite gates A and B is 7 m. Is it possible? If yes, where?
question_hinglish: 13 m diameter waale gol park ki boundary pe ek khamba aise lagaana hai ki aamne-saamne ke do gates A aur B se uski doori ka fark 7 m ho. Kya ye sambhav hai? Agar haan, toh kahaan?
answer_english:
Let BP = x m, AP = (x + 7) m. AB is a diameter, so ∠APB = 90°.
Pythagoras: (x + 7)² + x² = 13² → 2x² + 14x − 120 = 0 → x² + 7x − 60 = 0.
D = 49 + 240 = 289 > 0, so real roots exist and it is possible.
x = (−7 ± 17)/2 = 5 or −12; distance cannot be negative, so x = 5.
The pole is 5 m from gate B and 12 m from gate A.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: What is an arithmetic progression (AP)? What is its common difference and general form?
question_hinglish: Arithmetic progression (AP) kya hoti hai? Iska common difference aur general form kya hai?
answer_english:
An arithmetic progression is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term, except the first term.
The fixed number is the common difference d; it can be positive, negative or zero. d = aₖ₊₁ − aₖ.
General form: a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, …, where a is the first term.
Examples: 1, 2, 3, 4, … (d = 1); 100, 70, 40, 10, … (d = −30); 3, 3, 3, 3, … (d = 0).
answer_hinglish:
Arithmetic progression numbers ki aisi list hai jisme pehle term ko chhodkar har term pichhle term mein ek fixed number jodkar milta hai.
Ye fixed number common difference d hai; ye positive, negative ya zero ho sakta hai. d = aₖ₊₁ − aₖ.
General form: a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, …, jahan a pehla term hai.
Udaharan: 1, 2, 3, 4, … (d = 1); 100, 70, 40, 10, … (d = −30); 3, 3, 3, 3, … (d = 0).

This fixed number is called the common difference of the AP. Remember that it can be positive, negative or zero. Let us denote the first term of an AP by a₁, second term by a₂, . . ., nth term by aₙ and the common difference by d. You can see that a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, . . . represents an arithmetic progression where a is the first term and d the common difference. This is called the general form of an AP.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Derive the formula for the nth term of an AP using Reena's salary example.
question_hinglish: Reena ki salary ke udaharan se AP ke nth term ka formula nikaalo.
answer_english:
Reena's salary: 8000, 8500, 9000, … with increment 500.
3rd year = 8000 + 2 × 500 = 8000 + (3 − 1) × 500 = 9000; 5th year = 8000 + (5 − 1) × 500 = 10000; 15th year = 8000 + 14 × 500 = 15000.
In general: a₂ = a + d, a₃ = a + 2d, a₄ = a + 3d, so the nth term is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
aₙ is called the general term. If the AP has m terms, aₘ is the last term, often written l.
answer_hinglish:
Reena ki salary: 8000, 8500, 9000, …, badhotri 500.
Teesra saal = 8000 + 2 × 500 = 8000 + (3 − 1) × 500 = 9000; paanchva saal = 8000 + (5 − 1) × 500 = 10000; 15va saal = 8000 + 14 × 500 = 15000.
Aam taur pe: a₂ = a + d, a₃ = a + 2d, a₄ = a + 3d, toh nth term aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
aₙ ko general term kehte hain. Agar AP mein m terms hain, toh aₘ aakhri term hai, jise aksar l likhte hain.
ncert_context: Reena has been offered the job with a starting monthly salary of ₹8000, with an annual increment of ₹500. So, the salary for the 3rd year = ₹[8000 + (3 – 1) × 500] = ₹9000. Salary for the 5th year = ₹[8000 + (5 – 1) × 500] = ₹10000. Salary for the 15th year = ₹[8000 + (15 – 1) × 500] = ₹15000, i.e., First salary + (15 – 1) × Annual increment. Let a₁, a₂, a₃, . . . be an AP whose first term a₁ is a and the common difference is d. Then, the second term a₂ = a + d = a + (2 – 1) d, the third term a₃ = a + 2d = a + (3 – 1) d. Looking at the pattern, we can say that the nth term aₙ = a + (n – 1) d. aₙ is also called the general term of the AP. If there are m terms in the AP, then aₘ represents the last term which is sometimes also denoted by l.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: How did Gauss add 1 to 100, and how does the same idea give the sum of the first n terms of an AP?
question_hinglish: Gauss ne 1 se 100 tak kaise joda, aur wahi tareeka AP ke pehle n terms ka jod kaise deta hai?
answer_english:
Gauss wrote S = 1 + 2 + … + 100 and in reverse S = 100 + 99 + … + 1. Adding: 2S = 101 × 100, so S = 5050.
For an AP: S = a + (a + d) + … + [a + (n − 1)d], and reversed S = [a + (n − 1)d] + … + a.
Adding term-wise, each pair sums to 2a + (n − 1)d, and there are n pairs: 2S = n[2a + (n − 1)d].
So Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d] = (n/2)(a + l), where l is the last term. The second form is useful when d is not given.
Also, aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁.

(b) In a potato race the bucket is 5 m from the first potato, and ten potatoes are placed 3 m apart. Each potato is fetched separately. What is the total distance run?
question_hinglish: (a) 200 lakdiyaan aise rakhi hain: neeche ki line mein 20, agli mein 19, aur aise hi. Kitni lines hain aur sabse upar kitni lakdiyaan? (b) Potato race mein bucket pehle aaloo se 5 m door hai aur das aaloo 3 m ke fark pe hain. Har aaloo alag se laana hai. Kul kitna daudna padega?
answer_english:
(a) (n/2)[40 − (n − 1)] = 200 → n² − 41n + 400 = 0 → (n − 16)(n − 25) = 0. n = 25 would give a negative top row, so n = 16 rows; top row = 20 − 15 = 5 logs.
(b) Distances to the potatoes: 5, 8, 11, …, 32 m. Each is run twice: total = 2 × (10/2)(5 + 32) = 2 × 185 = 370 m.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: What are similar figures? How are they different from congruent figures?
question_hinglish: Similar figures kya hote hain? Ye congruent figures se kaise alag hain?
answer_english:
Similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size.
Congruent figures have the same shape and the same size.
So all congruent figures are similar, but similar figures need not be congruent.
Examples: all circles are similar, all squares are similar and all equilateral triangles are similar. A circle and a square are never similar.
answer_hinglish:

Congruent figures ka shape aur size dono same hote hain.
Isliye saare congruent figures similar hote hain, par similar figures congruent hon ye zaroori nahi.
Udaharan: saare circles similar hain, saare squares similar hain aur saare equilateral triangles similar hain. Circle aur square kabhi similar nahi hote.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: When are two polygons similar? Why is one condition alone not enough?
question_hinglish: Do polygons kab similar hote hain? Sirf ek shart kaafi kyun nahi hai?
answer_english:
Two polygons with the same number of sides are similar if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (proportion).
The common ratio is called the scale factor or Representative Fraction, as used in maps and blueprints.
Neither condition alone is enough:
- A square and a rectangle have equal angles (all 90°) but sides not in the same ratio → not similar.
- A square and a rhombus have sides in the same ratio but unequal angles → not similar.
answer_hinglish:
Same number of sides waale do polygons similar hain agar (i) unke corresponding angles barabar hon aur (ii) corresponding sides same ratio (proportion) mein hon.
Is common ratio ko scale factor ya Representative Fraction kehte hain, jo maps aur blueprints mein use hota hai.
Akeli koi bhi shart kaafi nahi:
- Square aur rectangle ke angles barabar (sab 90°) par sides same ratio mein nahi → similar nahi.
- Square aur rhombus ki sides same ratio mein par angles barabar nahi → similar nahi.
ncert_context: Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion). Note that the same ratio of the corresponding sides is referred to as the scale factor (or the Representative Fraction) for the polygons. You must have heard that world maps (i.e., global maps) and blue prints for the construction of a building are prepared using a suitable scale factor. You may note that in the two quadrilaterals (a square and a rectangle), corresponding angles are equal, but their corresponding sides are not in the same ratio. So, the two quadrilaterals are not similar. Similarly, you may note that in the two quadrilaterals (a square and a rhombus), corresponding sides are in the same ratio, but their corresponding angles are not equal. Thus, either of the above two conditions (i) and (ii) of similarity of two polygons is not sufficient for them to be similar.

question_english: How does a photographer's enlargement of photos illustrate similarity? Are two same-size photos of a person at age 10 and 40 similar?
question_hinglish: Photographer ka photo bada karna similarity ko kaise samjhaata hai? Kya ek insaan ki 10 aur 40 saal ki umar ki same size ki photos similar hain?
answer_english:
When a 35 mm photo is enlarged to 45 mm or 55 mm, every line segment is enlarged in the ratio 35 : 45 (or 35 : 55), and the angles between corresponding segments stay equal. So photos of different sizes from the same negative are similar, like three photos of the Taj Mahal in different sizes.
Photos of the same person at ages 10 and 40 may be the same size, but they are not the same shape, so they are not similar.
Heights of mountains and distances of far objects like the moon are also found indirectly using similarity.
answer_hinglish:
Jab 35 mm photo ko 45 mm ya 55 mm tak bada karte hain, toh har line segment 35 : 45 (ya 35 : 55) ke ratio mein badhta hai, aur corresponding segments ke beech ke angles barabar rehte hain. Isliye ek hi negative se bani alag size ki photos similar hain, jaise Taj Mahal ki teen alag size ki photos.
Ek hi insaan ki 10 aur 40 saal ki photos same size ki ho sakti hain, par shape same nahi, toh similar nahi hain.
Pahaadon ki oonchai aur chaand jaisi door ki cheezon ki doori bhi similarity se indirectly nikaali jaati hai.

question_english: State and prove the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales Theorem).
question_hinglish: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales Theorem) batao aur prove karo.
answer_english:
Theorem 6.1: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
Given: in △ABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. To prove: AD/DB = AE/EC.
Proof: join BE and CD; draw DM ⊥ AC and EN ⊥ AB.
ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = (½·AD·EN)/(½·DB·EN) = AD/DB …(1)
ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = (½·AE·DM)/(½·EC·DM) = AE/EC …(2)
△BDE and △DEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels BC and DE, so ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) …(3)
From (1), (2), (3): AD/DB = AE/EC.
answer_hinglish:
Theorem 6.1: Agar triangle ki ek side ke parallel ek line kheenchi jaaye jo baaki do sides ko alag points pe kaate, toh woh do sides same ratio mein bat jaati hain.
Diya hai: △ABC mein DE ∥ BC, D AB pe aur E AC pe. Prove karna hai: AD/DB = AE/EC.
Proof: BE aur CD jodo; DM ⊥ AC aur EN ⊥ AB kheencho.
ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = (½·AD·EN)/(½·DB·EN) = AD/DB …(1)
ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = (½·AE·DM)/(½·EC·DM) = AE/EC …(2)
△BDE aur △DEC ek hi base DE pe aur same parallels BC aur DE ke beech hain, toh ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) …(3)
(1), (2), (3) se: AD/DB = AE/EC.
ncert_context: Theorem 6.1: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio. Proof: We are given a triangle ABC in which a line parallel to side BC intersects other two sides AB and AC at D and E respectively. We need to prove that AD/DB = AE/EC. Let us join BE and CD and then draw DM ⊥ AC and EN ⊥ AB. ar(ADE) = ½ AD × EN. ar(BDE) = ½ DB × EN, ar(ADE) = ½ AE × DM and ar(DEC) = ½ EC × DM. Note that ΔBDE and DEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels BC and DE. So, ar(BDE) = ar(DEC). Therefore, AD/DB = AE/EC. A famous Greek mathematician Thales gave an important truth relating to two equiangular triangles. It is believed that he had used a result called the Basic Proportionality Theorem (now known as the Thales Theorem).

question_english: State the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem. How is it shown?
question_hinglish: Basic Proportionality Theorem ka converse batao. Ise kaise dikhaate hain?
answer_english:
Theorem 6.2: If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
Activity: on the arms of an angle, mark equal parts AB₁ = B₁B₂ = … and AC₁ = C₁C₂ = …; then AB₁/B₁B = AC₁/C₁C = 1/4 and B₁C₁ ∥ BC, and similarly for B₂C₂, B₃C₃, B₄C₄.
Proof idea: suppose AD/DB = AE/EC but DE is not parallel to BC. Draw DE′ ∥ BC; then AD/DB = AE′/E′C, so AE/EC = AE′/E′C. Adding 1 to both sides shows E and E′ coincide, so DE ∥ BC.

question_hinglish: (a) △ABC mein DE ∥ BC ho toh prove karo AD/AB = AE/AC. (b) ABCD trapezium hai jisme AB ∥ DC, aur EF ∥ AB jahan E AD pe aur F BC pe hai. Dikhao AE/ED = BF/FC.
answer_english:
(a) By BPT, AD/DB = AE/EC. Invert: DB/AD = EC/AE. Add 1: (DB + AD)/AD = (EC + AE)/AE → AB/AD = AC/AE. Invert: AD/AB = AE/AC.
(b) Join AC, meeting EF at G. EF ∥ AB ∥ DC.
In △ADC, EG ∥ DC → AE/ED = AG/GC …(1)
In △CAB, GF ∥ AB → CG/AG = CF/BF, i.e. AG/GC = BF/FC …(2)
From (1) and (2): AE/ED = BF/FC.

(b) AC jodo, jo EF ko G pe mile. EF ∥ AB ∥ DC.

△CAB mein GF ∥ AB → CG/AG = CF/BF, yaani AG/GC = BF/FC …(2)
(1) aur (2) se: AE/ED = BF/FC.

Therefore, from (1) and (2), AE/ED = BF/FC.

question_english: E and F are on sides PQ and PR of △PQR. Is EF ∥ QR? (i) PE = 3.9, EQ = 3, PF = 3.6, FR = 2.4 cm (ii) PE = 4, QE = 4.5, PF = 8, RF = 9 cm (iii) PQ = 1.28, PR = 2.56, PE = 0.18, PF = 0.36 cm
question_hinglish: △PQR ki sides PQ aur PR pe E aur F hain. Kya EF ∥ QR hai? (i) PE = 3.9, EQ = 3, PF = 3.6, FR = 2.4 cm (ii) PE = 4, QE = 4.5, PF = 8, RF = 9 cm (iii) PQ = 1.28, PR = 2.56, PE = 0.18, PF = 0.36 cm
answer_english:
Use the converse of BPT: EF ∥ QR only if the two sides are divided in the same ratio.
(i) PE/EQ = 3.9/3 = 1.3; PF/FR = 3.6/2.4 = 1.5. Not equal → EF is not parallel to QR.
(ii) PE/EQ = 4/4.5 = 8/9; PF/FR = 8/9. Equal → EF ∥ QR.
(iii) PE/PQ = 0.18/1.28 = 9/64; PF/PR = 0.36/2.56 = 9/64. Equal → EF ∥ QR.
answer_hinglish:
BPT ka converse lagao: EF ∥ QR tabhi jab dono sides same ratio mein batein.
(i) PE/EQ = 3.9/3 = 1.3; PF/FR = 3.6/2.4 = 1.5. Barabar nahi → EF, QR ke parallel nahi.
(ii) PE/EQ = 4/4.5 = 8/9; PF/FR = 8/9. Barabar → EF ∥ QR.
(iii) PE/PQ = 0.18/1.28 = 9/64; PF/PR = 0.36/2.56 = 9/64. Barabar → EF ∥ QR.

question_english: (a) Using Theorem 6.1, prove that a line through the mid-point of one side of a triangle parallel to another side bisects the third side. (b) ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC whose diagonals meet at O. Show AO/BO = CO/DO.
question_hinglish: (a) Theorem 6.1 se prove karo ki triangle ki ek side ke mid-point se doosri side ke parallel kheenchi line teesri side ko bisect karti hai. (b) ABCD trapezium hai, AB ∥ DC, aur diagonals O pe milte hain. Dikhao AO/BO = CO/DO.
answer_english:
(a) In △ABC, D is the mid-point of AB, so AD/DB = 1. DE ∥ BC meets AC at E. By BPT, AE/EC = AD/DB = 1, so AE = EC, i.e. E is the mid-point of AC.
(b) In △AOB and △COD: ∠OAB = ∠OCD and ∠OBA = ∠ODC (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC). So △AOB ~ △COD (AA).
Hence AO/CO = BO/DO, i.e. AO/BO = CO/DO.
answer_hinglish:
(a) △ABC mein D, AB ka mid-point hai, toh AD/DB = 1. DE ∥ BC, AC ko E pe milti hai. BPT se, AE/EC = AD/DB = 1, toh AE = EC, yaani E, AC ka mid-point hai.
(b) △AOB aur △COD mein: ∠OAB = ∠OCD aur ∠OBA = ∠ODC (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC). Toh △AOB ~ △COD (AA).
Isliye AO/CO = BO/DO, yaani AO/BO = CO/DO.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: List the criteria for similarity of two triangles.
question_hinglish: Do triangles ki similarity ke criteria batao.
answer_english:
1. AAA: if corresponding angles are equal, the corresponding sides are proportional and the triangles are similar.
2. AA: if two angles of one triangle equal two angles of the other, the third angles are also equal (angle sum property), so the triangles are similar.
3. SSS: if corresponding sides are in the same ratio, the corresponding angles are equal and the triangles are similar.
4. SAS: if one angle of a triangle equals one angle of the other and the sides including these angles are proportional, the triangles are similar.
5. RHS: in two right triangles, if the hypotenuse and one side are proportional, the triangles are similar.
answer_hinglish:
1. AAA: corresponding angles barabar hon toh corresponding sides proportional hoti hain aur triangles similar hain.
2. AA: ek triangle ke do angles doosre ke do angles ke barabar hon toh teesra angle bhi barabar hoga (angle sum property), toh triangles similar hain.
3. SSS: corresponding sides same ratio mein hon toh corresponding angles barabar hain aur triangles similar hain.
4. SAS: ek angle barabar ho aur us angle ko banaane waali sides proportional hon toh triangles similar hain.
5. RHS: do right triangles mein hypotenuse aur ek side proportional hon toh triangles similar hain.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: For polygons both conditions (equal angles and proportional sides) are needed for similarity. Why is one enough for triangles? How should △ABC ~ △DEF be written?
question_hinglish: Polygons ki similarity ke liye dono shartein (barabar angles aur proportional sides) chahiye. Triangles ke liye ek kaafi kyun hai? △ABC ~ △DEF kaise likhte hain?
answer_english:
For triangles, Theorem 6.3 (AAA) shows equal angles force proportional sides, and Theorem 6.4 (SSS) shows proportional sides force equal angles. So one condition implies the other and only one needs checking. For general polygons this fails (e.g. a square vs a rectangle or rhombus).
Notation: '△ABC ~ △DEF' means A ↔ D, B ↔ E, C ↔ F. Vertices must be written in the correct correspondence. △ABC ~ △EDF is wrong, but △BAC ~ △EDF is fine. The symbol '~' means 'is similar to', while '≅' means 'is congruent to'.
answer_hinglish:
Triangles ke liye Theorem 6.3 (AAA) dikhata hai ki barabar angles se sides proportional ho jaati hain, aur Theorem 6.4 (SSS) dikhata hai ki proportional sides se angles barabar ho jaate hain. Toh ek shart doosri ko imply karti hai aur ek hi jaanchni padti hai. Aam polygons mein aisa nahi hota (jaise square vs rectangle ya rhombus).
Notation: '△ABC ~ △DEF' ka matlab A ↔ D, B ↔ E, C ↔ F. Vertices sahi correspondence mein likhne chahiye. △ABC ~ △EDF galat hai, par △BAC ~ △EDF sahi hai. '~' ka matlab 'similar hai', jabki '≅' ka matlab 'congruent hai'.

Symbolically, we write the similarity of these two triangles as 'Δ ABC ~ Δ DEF' and read it as 'triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF'. The symbol '~' stands for 'is similar to'. For example, we cannot write Δ ABC ~ Δ EDF or Δ ABC ~ Δ FED. However, we can write Δ BAC ~ Δ EDF.

question_english: (a) If PQ ∥ RS and PS, QR meet at O, prove △POQ ~ △SOR. (b) If OA·OB = OC·OD (AC and BD meeting at O), show ∠A = ∠C and ∠B = ∠D.
question_hinglish: (a) Agar PQ ∥ RS aur PS, QR, O pe milte hain, toh prove karo △POQ ~ △SOR. (b) Agar OA·OB = OC·OD (AC aur BD, O pe milte hain), toh dikhao ∠A = ∠C aur ∠B = ∠D.
answer_english:
(a) PQ ∥ RS, so ∠P = ∠S and ∠Q = ∠R (alternate angles). Also ∠POQ = ∠SOR (vertically opposite). So △POQ ~ △SOR (AAA).

From (1) and (2), △AOD ~ △COB (SAS). So ∠A = ∠C and ∠D = ∠B (corresponding angles of similar triangles).

question_english: A girl 90 cm tall walks away from a lamp-post at 1.2 m/s. The lamp is 3.6 m above the ground. Find the length of her shadow after 4 seconds.
question_hinglish: 90 cm lambi ladki lamp-post se 1.2 m/s ki speed se door chal rahi hai. Lamp zameen se 3.6 m upar hai. 4 second baad uski parchhaai ki lambai nikaalo.
answer_english:
Distance walked BD = 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 m. Let the shadow DE = x m.
In △ABE (lamp-post) and △CDE (girl): ∠B = ∠D = 90° and ∠E is common, so △ABE ~ △CDE (AA).
BE/DE = AB/CD → (4.8 + x)/x = 3.6/0.9 = 4 → 4.8 + x = 4x → x = 1.6.
Her shadow is 1.6 m long.

(ii) From (i), CM/RN = CA/RP, and CA/RP = AB/PQ from (1). So CM/RN = AB/PQ.
So the ratio of medians equals the ratio of corresponding sides.

subject: Mathematics
question_english:
Assertion (A): Two triangles with sides 3, 6, 8 cm and 4.5, 9, 12 cm have equal corresponding angles.
Reason (R): If the sides of one triangle are proportional to the sides of another, their corresponding angles are equal.
question_hinglish:
Assertion (A): 3, 6, 8 cm aur 4.5, 9, 12 cm sides waale do triangles ke corresponding angles barabar hain.
Reason (R): Agar ek triangle ki sides doosre ki sides ke proportional hon, toh unke corresponding angles barabar hote hain.
answer_english:
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
3/4.5 = 6/9 = 8/12 = 2/3, so the sides are proportional. By the SSS similarity criterion (Theorem 6.4), the corresponding angles are equal.
answer_hinglish:
A aur R dono sahi hain, aur R, A ki sahi vyakhya hai.
3/4.5 = 6/9 = 8/12 = 2/3, toh sides proportional hain. SSS similarity criterion (Theorem 6.4) se corresponding angles barabar hain.
ncert_context: Activity 5: Draw two triangles ABC and DEF such that AB = 3 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 8 cm, DE = 4.5 cm, EF = 9 cm and FD = 12 cm. So, you have: AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD (each equal to 2/3). Now measure ∠ A, ∠ B, ∠ C, ∠ D, ∠ E and ∠ F. You will observe that ∠ A = ∠ D, ∠ B = ∠ E and ∠ C = ∠ F, i.e., the corresponding angles of the two triangles are equal. Theorem 6.4: If in two triangles, sides of one triangle are proportional to (i.e., in the same ratio of) the sides of the other triangle, then their corresponding angles are equal and hence the two triangles are similiar. This criterion is referred to as the SSS (Side–Side–Side) similarity criterion for two triangles.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: True or False: (i) All congruent figures are similar. (ii) All similar figures are congruent. (iii) Two isosceles triangles are always similar.
question_hinglish: Sahi ya Galat: (i) Saare congruent figures similar hote hain. (ii) Saare similar figures congruent hote hain. (iii) Do isosceles triangles hamesha similar hote hain.
answer_english:
(i) True: congruent figures have the same shape and size, so in particular the same shape.
(ii) False: similar figures need not be the same size, e.g. two circles of different radii.
(iii) False: two isosceles triangles can have different vertex angles (e.g. 40° and 100°), so their angles need not be equal. Only all equilateral triangles are always similar.
answer_hinglish:
(i) Sahi: congruent figures ka shape aur size same hota hai, toh shape bhi same hai.
(ii) Galat: similar figures ka size same hona zaroori nahi, jaise alag radius ke do circles.
(iii) Galat: do isosceles triangles ke vertex angles alag ho sakte hain (jaise 40° aur 100°), toh angles barabar nahi bhi ho sakte. Sirf saare equilateral triangles hamesha similar hote hain.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Why is coordinate geometry useful, and where is it applied?
question_hinglish: Coordinate geometry kyun upyogi hai, aur kahaan use hoti hai?
answer_english:
Coordinate geometry was developed as an algebraic tool for studying the geometry of figures. It lets us study geometry using algebra, and understand algebra with the help of geometry. For example, ax + by + c = 0 is a straight line and y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola.
It is widely applied in physics, engineering, navigation, seismology and art.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Derive the distance formula between P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂).
question_hinglish: P(x₁, y₁) aur Q(x₂, y₂) ke beech ka distance formula nikaalo.
answer_english:
Draw PR and QS perpendicular to the x-axis, and PT perpendicular to QS.
Then OR = x₁ and OS = x₂, so PT = RS = x₂ − x₁. Also QT = SQ − ST = y₂ − y₁.
By Pythagoras in right △PTQ: PQ² = PT² + QT² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)².
So PQ = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]. Only the positive root is taken, since distance is non-negative.
The distance of P(x, y) from the origin is √(x² + y²). Also PQ = √[(x₁ − x₂)² + (y₁ − y₂)²], since squares ignore sign.

Now, applying the Pythagoras theorem in Δ PTQ, we get PQ² = PT² + QT² = (x₂ – x₁)² + (y₂ – y₁)². Therefore, PQ = √[(x₂ – x₁)² + (y₂ – y₁)²]. question_english: Do the points (3, 2), (−2, −3) and (2, 3) form a triangle? If so, what type?
question_hinglish: Kya points (3, 2), (−2, −3) aur (2, 3) triangle banaate hain? Agar haan, toh kaisa?
answer_english:
P(3, 2), Q(−2, −3), R(2, 3).
PQ = √(25 + 25) = √50 ≈ 7.07; QR = √(16 + 36) = √52 ≈ 7.21; PR = √(1 + 1) = √2 ≈ 1.41.
The sum of any two distances exceeds the third, so they form a triangle.
Also PQ² + PR² = 50 + 2 = 52 = QR², so by the converse of Pythagoras ∠P = 90°. It is a right triangle.

question_english: Show that (1, 7), (4, 2), (−1, −1) and (−4, 4) are the vertices of a square.
question_hinglish: Dikhao ki (1, 7), (4, 2), (−1, −1) aur (−4, 4) ek square ke vertices hain.
answer_english:
A(1, 7), B(4, 2), C(−1, −1), D(−4, 4).
AB = √(9 + 25) = √34, BC = √(25 + 9) = √34, CD = √(9 + 25) = √34, DA = √(25 + 9) = √34.
Diagonals: AC = √(4 + 64) = √68, BD = √(64 + 4) = √68.

Alternatively, AD² + DC² = 34 + 34 = 68 = AC², so ∠D = 90°; a quadrilateral with four equal sides and one right angle is a square.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: State the section formula and the mid-point formula. Derive the section formula briefly.
question_hinglish: Section formula aur mid-point formula batao. Section formula sankshep mein nikaalo.
answer_english:
If P(x, y) divides the join of A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) internally in the ratio m₁ : m₂ (PA : PB = m₁ : m₂), then
P = ((m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁ + m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁ + m₂)).
Derivation: draw AR, PS, BT ⊥ x-axis and AQ, PC ∥ x-axis. △PAQ ~ △BPC (AA), so m₁/m₂ = PA/BP = AQ/PC = PQ/BC = (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x) = (y − y₁)/(y₂ − y). Solving each gives x and y.
For ratio k : 1: P = ((kx₂ + x₁)/(k + 1), (ky₂ + y₁)/(k + 1)).
Mid-point (ratio 1 : 1): ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).

P = ((m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁ + m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁ + m₂)).

question_english: (a) A(6, 1), B(8, 2), C(9, 4), D(p, 3) form a parallelogram in order; find p. (b) (1, 2), (4, y), (x, 6), (3, 5) form a parallelogram in order; find x and y. (c) AB is a diameter of a circle with centre (2, −3) and B(1, 4); find A.
question_hinglish: (a) A(6, 1), B(8, 2), C(9, 4), D(p, 3) kram se parallelogram banaate hain; p nikaalo. (b) (1, 2), (4, y), (x, 6), (3, 5) kram se parallelogram hain; x aur y nikaalo. (c) AB ek circle ka diameter hai jiska centre (2, −3) aur B(1, 4) hai; A nikaalo.
answer_english:
The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so the mid-points of the diagonals coincide.
(a) Mid AC = (15/2, 5/2) = mid BD = ((8 + p)/2, 5/2) → p = 7.
(b) Mid of (1, 2)–(x, 6) = mid of (4, y)–(3, 5): (1 + x)/2 = 7/2 → x = 6; 8/2 = (y + 5)/2 → y = 3.
(c) The centre is the mid-point of AB: A = (2·2 − 1, 2·(−3) − 4) = (3, −10).

question_english: On a school ground, lines are drawn 1 m apart and 100 flower pots are placed 1 m apart along AD. Niharika runs 1/4 of AD on the 2nd line and posts a green flag; Preet runs 1/5 of AD on the 8th line and posts a red flag. Find the distance between the flags and where Rashmi should post a blue flag halfway between them.
question_hinglish: School ground pe lines 1 m ke fark pe hain aur AD ke saath 100 gamle 1 m ke fark pe rakhe hain. Niharika doosri line pe AD ka 1/4 daudkar hari jhandi lagaati hai; Preet aathvi line pe AD ka 1/5 daudkar laal jhandi lagaata hai. Jhandiyon ki doori aur Rashmi ki neeli jhandi ki jagah (theek beech mein) nikaalo.
answer_english:
AD = 100 m. Take the line number as x and the distance along AD as y.
Green flag: (2, 100/4) = (2, 25). Red flag: (8, 100/5) = (8, 20).
Distance = √[(8 − 2)² + (20 − 25)²] = √(36 + 25) = √61 m ≈ 7.81 m.
Blue flag at the mid-point: ((2 + 8)/2, (25 + 20)/2) = (5, 22.5), i.e. on the 5th line, 22.5 m along AD.

question_hinglish: Trigonometry kya hai? Ye shabd kahaan se aaya?
answer_english:
Trigonometry is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle.
The word comes from the Greek 'tri' (three), 'gon' (sides) and 'metron' (measure).

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Define the six trigonometric ratios of angle A in a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B.
question_hinglish: B pe right-angled triangle ABC mein angle A ke chhe trigonometric ratios define karo.
answer_english:
BC is opposite to ∠A, AB is adjacent to ∠A, and AC is the hypotenuse.
sin A = opposite/hypotenuse = BC/AC
cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse = AB/AC
tan A = opposite/adjacent = BC/AB
cosec A = 1/sin A = AC/BC
sec A = 1/cos A = AC/AB
cot A = 1/tan A = AB/BC
Also tan A = sin A/cos A and cot A = cos A/sin A.

tan A = opposite/adjacent = BC/AB

Saath hi tan A = sin A/cos A aur cot A = cos A/sin A.
ncert_context: Here, ∠ CAB (or, in brief, angle A) is an acute angle. Note the position of the side BC with respect to angle A. It faces ∠ A. We call it the side opposite to angle A. AC is the hypotenuse of the right triangle and the side AB is a part of ∠ A. So, we call it the side adjacent to angle A. The trigonometric ratios of the angle A in right triangle ABC are defined as follows: sine of ∠ A = side opposite to angle A/hypotenuse = BC/AC, cosine of ∠ A = side adjacent to angle A/hypotenuse = AB/AC, tangent of ∠ A = side opposite to angle A/side adjacent to angle A = BC/AB, cosecant of ∠ A = 1/sine of ∠ A = AC/BC, secant of ∠ A = 1/cosine of ∠ A = AC/AB, cotangent of ∠ A = 1/tangent of ∠ A = AB/BC. Note that the ratios cosec A, sec A and cot A are respectively, the reciprocals of the ratios sin A, cos A and tan A. Also, observe that tan A = sin A/cos A and cot A = cos A/sin A.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: How did the words 'sine' and 'cosine' originate?
question_hinglish: 'Sine' aur 'cosine' shabd kaise bane?
answer_english:
Aryabhata first used the idea of sine as we use it today in the Aryabhatiyam (A.D. 500). He called the half-chord ardha-jya, later shortened to jya or jiva.
In the Arabic translation jiva was kept as it was. In the Latin translation it became sinus (meaning curve), which spread through Europe as 'sine'. Edmund Gunter (1581–1626) first used the abbreviation 'sin'.
Cosine arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle; Aryabhata called it kotijya. The name cosinus came from Edmund Gunter, and Sir Jonas Moore first used 'cos' in 1674.
answer_hinglish:
Aryabhata ne Aryabhatiyam (A.D. 500) mein sine ka aaj jaisa upyog pehli baar kiya. Unhone aadhe chord ko ardha-jya kaha, jo baad mein jya ya jiva ban gaya.
Arabic anuvaad mein jiva waise hi raha. Latin anuvaad mein ye sinus (matlab curve) bana, jo Europe mein 'sine' ke roop mein phaila. Edmund Gunter (1581–1626) ne pehli baar 'sin' likha.
Cosine complementary angle ka sine nikaalne ki zaroorat se aaya; Aryabhata ne ise kotijya kaha. Naam cosinus Edmund Gunter se aaya, aur Sir Jonas Moore ne 1674 mein pehli baar 'cos' likha.
ncert_context: The first use of the idea of 'sine' in the way we use it today was in the work Aryabhatiyam by Aryabhata, in A.D. 500. Aryabhata used the word ardha-jya for the half-chord, which was shortened to jya or jiva in due course. When the Aryabhatiyam was translated into Arabic, the word jiva was retained as it is. The word jiva was translated into sinus, which means curve, when the Arabic version was translated into Latin. Soon the word sinus, also used as sine, became common in mathematical texts throughout Europe. An English Professor of astronomy Edmund Gunter (1581–1626), first used the abbreviated notation 'sin'. The cosine function arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle. Aryabhatta called it kotijya. The name cosinus originated with Edmund Gunter. In 1674, the English Mathematician Sir Jonas Moore first used the abbreviated notation 'cos'.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Do trigonometric ratios of an angle depend on the size of the triangle? Explain.
question_hinglish: Kya kisi angle ke trigonometric ratios triangle ke size pe nirbhar karte hain? Samjhaao.
answer_english:
No. Take a point P on hypotenuse AC (or Q on AC extended) and draw PM ⊥ AB. △PAM ~ △CAB by AA similarity (common ∠A and a right angle).
So corresponding sides are proportional: AM/AB = AP/AC = MP/BC. This gives MP/AP = BC/AC = sin A, AM/AP = cos A, MP/AM = tan A, and so on.
Therefore the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides, as long as the angle stays the same.
answer_hinglish:
Nahi. Hypotenuse AC pe point P (ya AC ko badhaakar Q) lo aur PM ⊥ AB kheencho. △PAM ~ △CAB, AA similarity se (common ∠A aur ek right angle).
Toh corresponding sides proportional hain: AM/AB = AP/AC = MP/BC. Isse MP/AP = BC/AC = sin A, AM/AP = cos A, MP/AM = tan A, aadi milte hain.
Isliye angle same rahe toh trigonometric ratios sides ki lambai se nahi badalte.
ncert_context: Now, if we take a point P on the hypotenuse AC or a point Q on AC extended, of the right triangle ABC and draw PM perpendicular to AB and QN perpendicular to AB extended, how will the trigonometric ratios of ∠ A in Δ PAM differ from those of ∠ A in Δ CAB or from those of ∠ A in Δ QAN? Using the criterion, you will see that the triangles PAM and CAB are similar. Therefore, by the property of similar triangles, the corresponding sides of the triangles are proportional. So, we have AM/AB = AP/AC = MP/BC. From this, we find MP/AP = BC/AC = sin A. Similarly, AM/AP = AB/AC = cos A, MP/AM = BC/AB = tan A and so on. From our observations, it is now clear that the values of the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if the angle remains the same.

(i) False: tan 60° = √3 > 1. tan A can exceed 1 when the opposite side is longer than the adjacent side.
(ii) True: sec A = hypotenuse/adjacent ≥ 1, and 12/5 > 1 (e.g. a triangle with adjacent 5, hypotenuse 12).

(iv) False: cot A is one symbol meaning 'cotangent of A'; 'cot' alone has no meaning.
(v) False: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse can never exceed 1, because the hypotenuse is the longest side.

cos A = 2√2k/3k = 2√2/3.

answer_english:

question_hinglish: 0° aur 90° ke trigonometric ratios kaise define hote hain? Kaun se define nahi hote?

As ∠A shrinks towards 0°, BC → 0 and AC → AB, so sin A → 0 and cos A → 1. We define sin 0° = 0 and cos 0° = 1. Then tan 0° = 0 and sec 0° = 1, while cot 0° and cosec 0° are not defined (division by zero).
As ∠A grows towards 90°, AB → 0 and AC → BC, so sin A → 1 and cos A → 0. We define sin 90° = 1 and cos 90° = 0. Then cosec 90° = 1 and cot 90° = 0, while tan 90° and sec 90° are not defined.
As A goes from 0° to 90°, sin A increases from 0 to 1 and cos A decreases from 1 to 0.

A 0° se 90° jaata hai toh sin A 0 se 1 tak badhta hai aur cos A 1 se 0 tak ghatta hai.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: What is a trigonometric identity? Derive the three fundamental identities and state where each holds.
question_hinglish: Trigonometric identity kya hai? Teen mool identities nikaalo aur batao har ek kahaan sahi hai.
answer_english:
A trigonometric identity is an equation in trigonometric ratios that is true for all values of the angle(s) involved.
In △ABC right-angled at B: AB² + BC² = AC² …(1)
Divide by AC²: (AB/AC)² + (BC/AC)² = 1 → cos²A + sin²A = 1, true for 0° ≤ A ≤ 90°.
Divide by AB²: 1 + (BC/AB)² = (AC/AB)² → 1 + tan²A = sec²A, true for 0° ≤ A < 90° (tan and sec are undefined at 90°).
Divide by BC²: (AB/BC)² + 1 = (AC/BC)² → cot²A + 1 = cosec²A, true for 0° < A ≤ 90° (cot and cosec are undefined at 0°).

ncert_context: An equation involving trigonometric ratios of an angle is called a trigonometric identity, if it is true for all values of the angle(s) involved. In Δ ABC, right-angled at B, we have: AB² + BC² = AC² (1). Dividing each term of (1) by AC², we get (AB/AC)² + (BC/AC)² = (AC/AC)², i.e., cos² A + sin² A = 1 (2). This is true for all A such that 0° ≤ A ≤ 90°. Let us now divide (1) by AB². 1 + tan² A = sec² A (3). tan A and sec A are not defined for A = 90°. So, (3) is true for all A such that 0° ≤ A < 90°. Dividing (1) by BC², cot² A + 1 = cosec² A (4). Note that cosec A and cot A are not defined for A = 0°. Therefore (4) is true for all A such that 0° < A ≤ 90°.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Define line of sight, angle of elevation and angle of depression.
question_hinglish: Line of sight, angle of elevation aur angle of depression define karo.
answer_english:
Line of sight: the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object being viewed.
Angle of elevation: the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal when the point is above the horizontal level (we raise our head), e.g. a student looking at the top of the Qutub Minar.
Angle of depression: the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal when the point is below the horizontal level (we lower our head), e.g. a girl on a balcony looking down at a flower pot.
answer_hinglish:
Line of sight: dekhne waale ki aankh se dekhi ja rahi cheez ke point tak kheenchi line.
Angle of elevation: line of sight aur horizontal ke beech ka angle jab point horizontal level se upar ho (hum sar uthaate hain), jaise student Qutub Minar ki chot ko dekh raha ho.
Angle of depression: line of sight aur horizontal ke beech ka angle jab point horizontal level se neeche ho (hum sar jhukaate hain), jaise balcony pe baithi ladki neeche gamle ko dekh rahi ho.
ncert_context: In this figure, the line AC drawn from the eye of the student to the top of the minar is called the line of sight. The angle BAC, so formed by the line of sight with the horizontal, is called the angle of elevation of the top of the minar from the eye of the student. Thus, the line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object viewed by the observer. The angle of elevation of the point viewed is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the point being viewed is above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise our head to look at the object. The girl sitting on the balcony is looking down at a flower pot placed on a stair of the temple. In this case, the line of sight is below the horizontal level. The angle so formed by the line of sight with the horizontal is called the angle of depression.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: To find the height of a minar without measuring it, what information is needed, and how is it used?
question_hinglish: Minar ki oonchai bina naape nikaalne ke liye kya jaankari chahiye, aur use kaise lagaate hain?
answer_english:
You need: (i) the distance DE of the student from the foot of the minar, (ii) the angle of elevation ∠BAC of the top, and (iii) the height AE of the student.
The height is CD = CB + BD, where BD = AE (the student's height).
In right △ABC, BC is opposite the known ∠A and AB = DE is adjacent, so use tan A = BC/AB (or cot A) to find BC.
Then height of minar = BC + AE.
answer_hinglish:
Chahiye: (i) minar ke paaye se student ki doori DE, (ii) chot ka angle of elevation ∠BAC, aur (iii) student ki oonchai AE.
Oonchai CD = CB + BD, jahan BD = AE (student ki oonchai).
Right △ABC mein BC, jaane hue ∠A ke saamne hai aur AB = DE paas mein, toh BC nikaalne ke liye tan A = BC/AB (ya cot A) lagao.
Phir minar ki oonchai = BC + AE.
ncert_context: If you want to find the height CD of the minar without actually measuring it, what information do you need? You would need to know the following: (i) the distance DE at which the student is standing from the foot of the minar (ii) the angle of elevation, ∠ BAC, of the top of the minar (iii) the height AE of the student. In the figure, CD = CB + BD. Here, BD = AE, which is the height of the student. To find BC, we will use trigonometric ratios of ∠ BAC or ∠ A. In Δ ABC, the side BC is the opposite side in relation to the known ∠ A. Our search narrows down to using either tan A or cot A, as these ratios involve AB and BC. Therefore, tan A = BC/AB or cot A = AB/BC, which on solving would give us BC. By adding AE to BC, you will get the height of the minar.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: (a) From a point 15 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of its top is 60°. Find the tower's height. (b) An observer 1.5 m tall is 28.5 m from a chimney and sees its top at 45°. Find the chimney's height.
question_hinglish: (a) Tower ke paaye se 15 m door point se uski chot ka angle of elevation 60° hai. Tower ki oonchai nikaalo. (b) 1.5 m lamba observer chimney se 28.5 m door hai aur uski chot 45° pe dekhta hai. Chimney ki oonchai nikaalo.
answer_english:
(a) tan 60° = AB/15 → √3 = AB/15 → AB = 15√3 m.
(b) Above eye level: tan 45° = AE/28.5 → AE = 28.5 m.
Chimney height = 28.5 + 1.5 = 30 m.
answer_hinglish:
(a) tan 60° = AB/15 → √3 = AB/15 → AB = 15√3 m.
(b) Aankh ke level se upar: tan 45° = AE/28.5 → AE = 28.5 m.
Chimney ki oonchai = 28.5 + 1.5 = 30 m.
ncert_context: Example 1: A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground, which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is found to be 60°. Find the height of the tower. tan 60° = AB/BC, i.e., √3 = AB/15, i.e., AB = 15√3. Hence, the height of the tower is 15√3 m. Example 3: An observer 1.5 m tall is 28.5 m away from a chimney. The angle of elevation of the top of the chimney from her eyes is 45°. What is the height of the chimney? AB = AE + BE = AE + 1.5 and DE = CB = 28.5 m. tan 45° = AE/DE, i.e., 1 = AE/28.5. Therefore, AE = 28.5. So the height of the chimney (AB) = (28.5 + 1.5) m = 30 m.

question_english: From the top of a multi-storeyed building, the angles of depression of the top and bottom of an 8 m building are 30° and 45°. Find the height of the multi-storeyed building and the distance between them.
question_hinglish: Ek oonchi building ki chot se 8 m building ki chot aur paaye ke angles of depression 30° aur 45° hain. Oonchi building ki oonchai aur dono ke beech ki doori nikaalo.
answer_english:
The angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from below (alternate angles), so ∠PBD = 30° and ∠PAC = 45°.
In △PBD: BD = √3·PD. In △PAC: PC = AC.
PC = PD + 8 and AC = BD, so PD + 8 = √3·PD → PD = 8/(√3 − 1) = 4(√3 + 1).
Height PC = 4(√3 + 1) + 8 = 4(3 + √3) m. Distance AC = PC = 4(3 + √3) m.

question_hinglish: (a) 50 m tower ke paaye se building ki chot 30° pe, aur building ke paaye se tower ki chot 60° pe dikhti hai. Building ki oonchai nikaalo. (b) 80 m sadak ke dono taraf do barabar khambe hain. Beech ke ek point se unki choten 60° aur 30° pe dikhti hain. Oonchai aur khambon se dooriyaan nikaalo.
answer_english:
(a) Distance d: tan 60° = 50/d → d = 50/√3. Building: tan 30° = h/d → h = (50/√3)(1/√3) = 50/3 = 16⅔ m.
(b) Let the point be x m from the first pole: h = x√3 and h = (80 − x)/√3.
So 3x = 80 − x → x = 20. Height = 20√3 m; distances 20 m and 60 m.

question_english: (a) From a 75 m lighthouse, two ships one behind the other are seen at depressions 30° and 45°. Find the distance between them. (b) A 1.2 m girl sees a balloon at 88.2 m height at 60°, and later at 30°. How far did it travel?
question_hinglish: (a) 75 m lighthouse se ek ke peeche ek do jahaaz 30° aur 45° depression pe dikhte hain. Unke beech ki doori nikaalo. (b) 1.2 m ki ladki 88.2 m oonchai pe gubbara 60° pe, aur baad mein 30° pe dekhti hai. Gubbara kitna chala?
answer_english:
(a) Near ship (45°): 75 m away. Far ship (30°): 75√3 m away.
Distance = 75√3 − 75 = 75(√3 − 1) m ≈ 54.9 m.
(b) Height above her eyes = 88.2 − 1.2 = 87 m.
At 60°: 87/√3 = 29√3 m away. At 30°: 87√3 m away.
Distance travelled = 87√3 − 29√3 = 58√3 m ≈ 100.5 m.

question_english: A man on a tower sees a car approaching at a 30° angle of depression; 6 seconds later it is at 60°. How long will the car take to reach the foot of the tower?
question_hinglish: Tower pe khada aadmi ek aati car ko 30° angle of depression pe dekhta hai; 6 second baad woh 60° pe hai. Car ko tower ke paaye tak pahunchne mein kitna samay lagega?
answer_english:
Let tower height = h.
At 30°: distance = h/tan 30° = h√3. At 60°: distance = h/tan 60° = h/√3.
Distance covered in 6 s = h√3 − h/√3 = 2h/√3.
Remaining distance = h/√3, which is half of 2h/√3.
At uniform speed it takes half the time: 6/2 = 3 seconds.

Bachi doori = h/√3, jo 2h/√3 ki aadhi hai.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Compare the angle of elevation and the angle of depression. Why are they equal for two observers looking at each other?
question_hinglish: Angle of elevation aur angle of depression ki tulna karo. Ek doosre ko dekhte do observers ke liye ye barabar kyun hote hain?
answer_english:
Angle of elevation: the line of sight is above the horizontal (looking up), e.g. from the ground to a tower top.
Angle of depression: the line of sight is below the horizontal (looking down), e.g. from a tower top to a car.
Both are measured from the horizontal through the observer's eye.
They are equal because the horizontal through the upper observer and the ground are parallel, and the line of sight is a transversal. The angle of depression (∠QPB) and the angle of elevation at the lower point (∠PBD) are alternate angles.
answer_hinglish:
Angle of elevation: line of sight horizontal se upar (upar dekhna), jaise zameen se tower ki chot.
Angle of depression: line of sight horizontal se neeche (neeche dekhna), jaise tower ki chot se car.
Dono observer ki aankh se guzarti horizontal se naape jaate hain.
Ye barabar hain kyunki upar waale observer ki horizontal aur zameen parallel hain, aur line of sight transversal hai. Angle of depression (∠QPB) aur neeche ke point ka angle of elevation (∠PBD) alternate angles hain.
ncert_context: The angle of elevation of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when it is above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise our head to look at the object. The angle of depression of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when it is below the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we lower our head to look at the object. Observe that PB is a transversal to the parallel lines PQ and BD. Therefore, ∠ QPB and ∠ PBD are alternate angles, and so are equal.

question_english: What are the three possible positions of a line with respect to a circle?
question_hinglish: Circle ke saapeksh ek line ki teen sambhav sthitiyaan kya hain?
answer_english:
1. Non-intersecting line: the line and the circle have no common point.
2. Secant: the line meets the circle at two points.
3. Tangent: the line meets the circle at exactly one point.
No other position is possible.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: What is a tangent to a circle? What is the point of contact, and where does the word 'tangent' come from?
question_hinglish: Circle ka tangent kya hota hai? Point of contact kya hai, aur 'tangent' shabd kahaan se aaya?
answer_english:
A tangent is a line that intersects the circle at exactly one point.
That common point is the point of contact, and the tangent is said to touch the circle there.
A tangent is a special case of a secant in which the two end points of its chord coincide.
The word comes from the Latin 'tangere' (to touch) and was introduced by the Danish mathematician Thomas Fineke in 1583.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Explain with activities that exactly one tangent exists at a point on a circle and at most two tangents can be parallel to a given secant.
question_hinglish: Activities se samjhaao ki circle ke ek point pe theek ek tangent hota hai aur kisi secant ke parallel zyada se zyada do tangents ho sakte hain.
answer_english:
Activity 1: attach a straight wire AB to a circular wire at P so it can rotate. In most positions it cuts the circle at P and a second point Q₁, Q₂, …. As it rotates, the second point moves closer to P, and in exactly one position it meets the circle only at P. So there is only one tangent at P.
Activity 2: draw lines parallel to a secant PQ on both sides. The chords they cut get shorter and shorter until the length becomes zero once on each side. These two positions are tangents parallel to PQ, so at most two tangents can be parallel to a given secant.
answer_hinglish:
Activity 1: gol taar pe P pe ek seedha taar AB jodo jo ghoom sake. Zyaadatar sthitiyon mein ye circle ko P aur ek doosre point Q₁, Q₂, … pe kaatta hai. Ghumaane pe doosra point P ke paas aata jaata hai, aur theek ek sthiti mein ye circle ko sirf P pe milta hai. Toh P pe sirf ek tangent hai.
Activity 2: secant PQ ke dono taraf parallel lines kheencho. Unki chords chhoti hoti jaati hain jab tak dono taraf ek-ek baar lambai zero na ho jaaye. Ye do sthitiyaan PQ ke parallel tangents hain, toh kisi secant ke parallel zyada se zyada do tangents ho sakte hain.
ncert_context: Activity 1: Take a circular wire and attach a straight wire AB at a point P of the circular wire so that it can rotate about the point P in a plane. In various positions, the wire intersects the circular wire at P and at another point Q₁ or Q₂ or Q₃, etc. In one position, you will see that it will intersect the circle at the point P only. This shows that a tangent exists at the point P of the circle. So, you can observe that there is only one tangent at a point of the circle. Activity 2: On a paper, draw a circle and a secant PQ of the circle. Draw various lines parallel to the secant on both sides of it. You will find that after some steps, the length of the chord cut by the lines will gradually decrease. In one case, it becomes zero on one side of the secant and in another case, it becomes zero on the other side of the secant. These are the tangents to the circle parallel to the given secant PQ. This also helps you to see that there cannot be more than two tangents parallel to a given secant.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: State and prove Theorem 10.1 about the tangent and the radius.
question_hinglish: Tangent aur radius ke baare mein Theorem 10.1 batao aur prove karo.
answer_english:
Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
Given: a circle with centre O and tangent XY at P. To prove: OP ⊥ XY.
Proof: take any point Q on XY other than P and join OQ. Q must lie outside the circle; otherwise XY would be a secant. So OQ > OP.
This holds for every point of XY except P, so OP is the shortest distance from O to XY. The shortest segment from a point to a line is the perpendicular, so OP ⊥ XY.
Consequences: there is one and only one tangent at any point of a circle. The line containing the radius through the point of contact is called the normal.
answer_hinglish:
Theorem 10.1: Circle ke kisi bhi point pe tangent, point of contact se guzarne waale radius pe perpendicular hota hai.
Diya hai: centre O waala circle aur P pe tangent XY. Prove karna hai: OP ⊥ XY.
Proof: XY pe P ke alawa koi point Q lo aur OQ jodo. Q circle ke bahar hi hoga; warna XY secant ban jaata. Toh OQ > OP.
Ye P ke alawa XY ke har point ke liye sahi hai, toh OP, O se XY tak ki sabse chhoti doori hai. Point se line tak sabse chhota segment perpendicular hota hai, toh OP ⊥ XY.
Nateeje: circle ke har point pe ek aur sirf ek tangent hota hai. Point of contact se guzarne waale radius ki line ko normal kehte hain.
ncert_context: Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. Proof: We are given a circle with centre O and a tangent XY to the circle at a point P. We need to prove that OP is perpendicular to XY. Take a point Q on XY other than P and join OQ. The point Q must lie outside the circle. (Note that if Q lies inside the circle, XY will become a secant and not a tangent to the circle). Therefore, OQ is longer than the radius OP of the circle. That is, OQ > OP. Since this happens for every point on the line XY except the point P, OP is the shortest of all the distances of the point O to the points of XY. So OP is perpendicular to XY. Remarks 1. By theorem above, we can also conclude that at any point on a circle there can be one and only one tangent. 2. The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also sometimes called the 'normal' to the circle at the point.

Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. Proof: We are given a circle with centre O and a tangent XY to the circle at a point P. We need to prove that OP is perpendicular to XY. Take a point Q on XY other than P and join OQ. The point Q must lie outside the circle. (Note that if Q lies inside the circle, XY will become a secant and not a tangent to the circle). Therefore, OQ is longer than the radius OP of the circle. That is, OQ > OP. Since this happens for every point on the line XY except the point P, OP is the shortest of all the distances of the point O to the points of XY. So OP is perpendicular to XY. Remarks 1. By theorem above, we can also conclude that at any point on a circle there can be one and only one tangent. 2. The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also sometimes called the 'normal' to the circle at the point.

Question:
State and prove Theorem 10.1 about the tangent and the radius.

Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
Given: a circle with centre O and tangent XY at P. To prove: OP ⊥ XY.
Proof: take any point Q on XY other than P and join OQ. Q must lie outside the circle; otherwise XY would be a secant. So OQ > OP.
This holds for every point of XY except P, so OP is the shortest distance from O to XY. The shortest segment from a point to a line is the perpendicular, so OP ⊥ XY.
Consequences: there is one and only one tangent at any point of a circle. The line containing the radius through the point of contact is called the normal.

question_english: Give everyday examples of tangents to a circle.
question_hinglish: Circle ke tangents ke rozmarra ke udaharan do.
answer_english:
1. The rope on either side of a pulley over a well, treated as a ray, is like a tangent to the circle of the pulley.
2. A bicycle or cart wheel moves along the ground, which is a tangent to the circle of the wheel. The radius (spoke) through the point of contact with the ground is at right angles to the ground, illustrating Theorem 10.1.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: How many tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point inside, on and outside the circle?
question_hinglish: Circle ke andar, circle pe aur circle ke bahar ke point se circle pe kitne tangents kheenche ja sakte hain?
answer_english:
Case 1: from a point inside the circle, none, since every line through it cuts the circle at two points.
Case 2: from a point on the circle, exactly one.
Case 3: from a point outside the circle, exactly two.
The length of the tangent from an external point P is the length of the segment from P to the point of contact.
answer_hinglish:
Case 1: andar ke point se, koi nahi, kyunki uss point se guzarti har line circle ko do points pe kaatti hai.
Case 2: circle pe ke point se, theek ek.
Case 3: bahar ke point se, theek do.
Bahar ke point P se tangent ki lambai, P se point of contact tak ke segment ki lambai hai.
ncert_context: Draw a circle on a paper. Take a point P inside it. You will find that all the lines through this point intersect the circle in two points. So, it is not possible to draw any tangent to a circle through a point inside it. Next take a point P on the circle. There is only one tangent to the circle at such a point. Finally, take a point P outside the circle. You will find that you can draw exactly two tangents to the circle through this point. Case 1: There is no tangent to a circle passing through a point lying inside the circle. Case 2: There is one and only one tangent to a circle passing through a point lying on the circle. Case 3: There are exactly two tangents to a circle through a point lying outside the circle. The length of the segment of the tangent from the external point P and the point of contact with the circle is called the length of the tangent from the point P to the circle.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Prove that the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. What else follows?
question_hinglish: Prove karo ki bahar ke point se circle pe kheenche gaye tangents ki lambaiyaan barabar hoti hain. Isse aur kya nikalta hai?
answer_english:
Theorem 10.2. Given: circle with centre O, external point P, tangents PQ and PR. To prove: PQ = PR.
Join OP, OQ, OR. ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90° (radius ⊥ tangent).
In right △OQP and △ORP: OQ = OR (radii) and OP = OP (common). So △OQP ≅ △ORP (RHS), giving PQ = PR (CPCT).
Alternatively, by Pythagoras: PQ² = OP² − OQ² = OP² − OR² = PR².
Also ∠OPQ = ∠OPR, so OP bisects ∠QPR: the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents.
answer_hinglish:
Theorem 10.2. Diya hai: centre O waala circle, bahar ka point P, tangents PQ aur PR. Prove karna hai: PQ = PR.
OP, OQ, OR jodo. ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90° (radius ⊥ tangent).
Right △OQP aur △ORP mein: OQ = OR (radii) aur OP = OP (common). Toh △OQP ≅ △ORP (RHS), jisse PQ = PR (CPCT).
Doosra tareeka, Pythagoras se: PQ² = OP² − OQ² = OP² − OR² = PR².
Saath hi ∠OPQ = ∠OPR, toh OP, ∠QPR ko bisect karta hai: centre dono tangents ke beech ke angle ke bisector pe hota hai.
ncert_context: Theorem 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. Proof: We are given a circle with centre O, a point P lying outside the circle and two tangents PQ, PR on the circle from P. We are required to prove that PQ = PR. For this, we join OP, OQ and OR. Then ∠ OQP and ∠ ORP are right angles, because these are angles between the radii and tangents, and according to Theorem 10.1 they are right angles. Now in right triangles OQP and ORP, OQ = OR (Radii of the same circle), OP = OP (Common). Therefore, Δ OQP ≅ Δ ORP (RHS). This gives PQ = PR (CPCT). Remarks 1. The theorem can also be proved by using the Pythagoras Theorem as follows: PQ² = OP² – OQ² = OP² – OR² = PR² (As OQ = OR) which gives PQ = PR. 2. Note also that ∠ OPQ = ∠ OPR. Therefore, OP is the angle bisector of ∠ QPR, i.e., the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents.

question_english: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ.
question_hinglish: Centre O waale circle pe bahar ke point T se do tangents TP aur TQ kheenche gaye. Prove karo ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ.

∠OPQ = ∠OPT − ∠TPQ = 90° − (90° − θ/2) = θ/2.
So ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ.

question_english: PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm. The tangents at P and Q meet at T. Find TP.
question_hinglish: PQ, 5 cm radius waale circle ki 8 cm lambi chord hai. P aur Q pe tangents T pe milte hain. TP nikaalo.
answer_english:
Join OT, meeting PQ at R. △TPQ is isosceles and TO bisects ∠PTQ, so OT ⊥ PQ and PR = RQ = 4 cm.
OR = √(5² − 4²) = 3 cm.
∠TPR + ∠RPO = 90° = ∠TPR + ∠PTR, so ∠RPO = ∠PTR. Hence right △TRP ~ right △PRO (AA).
TP/PO = RP/RO → TP/5 = 4/3 → TP = 20/3 cm.
Pythagoras check: with TR = y, x² = y² + 16 and x² + 25 = (y + 3)² give y = 16/3 and x = 20/3.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Prove: (a) tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel; (b) the perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact passes through the centre; (c) the angle between two tangents from an external point is supplementary to the angle subtended at the centre by the segment joining the points of contact.
question_hinglish: Prove karo: (a) diameter ke siron pe tangents parallel hote hain; (b) tangent ke point of contact pe perpendicular centre se guzarta hai; (c) bahar ke point se do tangents ke beech ka angle, points of contact ko jodne waale segment se centre pe bane angle ka supplementary hota hai.
answer_english:
(a) Let AB be a diameter with tangents at A and B. The radius OA ⊥ tangent at A and OB ⊥ tangent at B. So both tangents are perpendicular to the same line AB, and co-interior angles 90° + 90° = 180° make them parallel.
(b) The radius OP is ⊥ the tangent at P. At a point of a line only one perpendicular can be drawn in the plane, so the perpendicular at P must be the line OP, which passes through O.
(c) In quadrilateral OPTQ with tangents TP, TQ: ∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90°. So ∠PTQ + ∠POQ = 360° − 180° = 180°; they are supplementary.

(b) Radius OP, P pe tangent pe ⊥ hai. Line ke ek point pe plane mein sirf ek perpendicular ban sakta hai, toh P pe perpendicular line OP hi hai, jo O se guzarti hai.
(c) Tangents TP, TQ waale quadrilateral OPTQ mein: ∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90°. Toh ∠PTQ + ∠POQ = 360° − 180° = 180°; ye supplementary hain.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: (a) A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle. Prove AB + CD = AD + BC. (b) Hence prove that a parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
question_hinglish: (a) Quadrilateral ABCD ek circle ko gherta hai. Prove karo AB + CD = AD + BC. (b) Isse prove karo ki circle ko gherne waala parallelogram rhombus hota hai.
answer_english:
(a) Let the circle touch AB, BC, CD, DA at P, Q, R, S. Tangents from the same external point are equal: AP = AS, BP = BQ, CR = CQ, DR = DS.
Adding: (AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ), i.e. AB + CD = AD + BC.
(b) In a parallelogram, AB = CD and AD = BC. From (a), 2AB = 2AD, so AB = AD. All sides are then equal, so the parallelogram is a rhombus.
answer_hinglish:
(a) Maano circle AB, BC, CD, DA ko P, Q, R, S pe chhoota hai. Ek hi bahar ke point se tangents barabar hote hain: AP = AS, BP = BQ, CR = CQ, DR = DS.
Jodo: (AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ), yaani AB + CD = AD + BC.
(b) Parallelogram mein AB = CD aur AD = BC. (a) se 2AB = 2AD, toh AB = AD. Tab saari sides barabar hain, toh parallelogram rhombus hai.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: (a) The tangent from A, 5 cm from the centre, is 4 cm. Find the radius. (b) △ABC circumscribes a circle of radius 4 cm, and the point of contact D divides BC into BD = 8 cm and DC = 6 cm. Find AB and AC.
question_hinglish: (a) Centre se 5 cm door A se tangent 4 cm hai. Radius nikaalo. (b) △ABC, 4 cm radius waale circle ko gherta hai, aur contact point D, BC ko BD = 8 cm aur DC = 6 cm mein baantta hai. AB aur AC nikaalo.
answer_english:
(a) r = √(5² − 4²) = 3 cm.
(b) Let the tangent from A be x. Then AB = x + 8, AC = x + 6, BC = 14, and the semi-perimeter s = x + 14.
Area = r·s = 4(x + 14). By Heron's formula, area = √[(x + 14)(x)(8)(6)].
Squaring: 16(x + 14)² = 48x(x + 14) → x + 14 = 3x → x = 7.
AB = 15 cm, AC = 13 cm.

question_english: XY and X′Y′ are parallel tangents to a circle with centre O, and tangent AB at C meets XY at A and X′Y′ at B. Prove ∠AOB = 90°.
question_hinglish: XY aur X′Y′, centre O waale circle ke parallel tangents hain, aur C pe tangent AB, XY ko A pe aur X′Y′ ko B pe milta hai. Prove karo ∠AOB = 90°.
answer_english:
Let XY touch the circle at P and X′Y′ at Q. P, O, Q are collinear: PQ is a diameter, since both radii are ⊥ the parallel tangents.
From A, the tangents AP and AC are equal, so OA bisects ∠PAC. From B, OB bisects ∠QBC.
XY ∥ X′Y′ with transversal AB, so ∠PAB + ∠QBA = 180°.
Thus ∠OAB + ∠OBA = ½(180°) = 90°, and in △AOB, ∠AOB = 180° − 90° = 90°.

question_english: What are a sector and a segment of a circle? What are minor and major sectors and segments?
question_hinglish: Circle ka sector aur segment kya hota hai? Minor aur major sectors aur segments kya hain?
answer_english:
Sector: the part of the circular region enclosed by two radii and the corresponding arc. ∠AOB is the angle of the sector.
Segment: the part of the circular region enclosed between a chord and the corresponding arc.
The smaller one is the minor sector or segment and the larger one is the major sector or segment. The angle of the major sector is 360° − ∠AOB.
Unless stated otherwise, 'sector' and 'segment' mean the minor ones.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Derive the formulas for the area of a sector and the length of an arc of angle θ, and give the area of a segment.
question_hinglish: θ angle ke sector ka area aur arc ki lambai ke formulas nikaalo, aur segment ka area batao.
answer_english:
Unitary method: a full circle is a sector of 360° with area πr².
For 1°, the area is πr²/360; for θ°, area of sector = (θ/360) × πr².
Similarly, the whole circumference 2πr corresponds to 360°, so length of arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
Area of segment = area of sector − area of the corresponding triangle = (θ/360)πr² − area of △OAB.
Major sector = πr² − minor sector; major segment = πr² − minor segment.
answer_hinglish:
Unitary method: poora circle 360° ka sector hai jiska area πr² hai.
1° ke liye area πr²/360; θ° ke liye sector ka area = (θ/360) × πr².
Isi tarah poori paridhi 2πr, 360° ke barabar hai, toh arc ki lambai = (θ/360) × 2πr.
Segment ka area = sector ka area − sambandhit triangle ka area = (θ/360)πr² − △OAB ka area.
Major sector = πr² − minor sector; major segment = πr² − minor segment.
ncert_context: Let OAPB be a sector of a circle with centre O and radius r. Let the degree measure of ∠ AOB be θ. You know that area of a circle is πr². We can consider this circular region to be a sector forming an angle of 360° at the centre O. Now by applying the Unitary Method: When degree measure of the angle at the centre is 360, area of the sector = πr². So, when the degree measure of the angle at the centre is 1, area of the sector = πr²/360. Therefore, when the degree measure of the angle at the centre is θ, area of the sector = (θ/360) × πr². Taking the whole length of the circle (of angle 360°) as 2πr, length of an arc of a sector of angle θ = (θ/360) × 2πr. Area of the segment APB = Area of the sector OAPB – Area of Δ OAB = (θ/360) × πr² – area of Δ OAB. Area of the major sector OAQB = πr² – Area of the minor sector OAPB and Area of major segment AQB = πr² – Area of the minor segment APB.

question_english: A round table cover of radius 28 cm has six equal designs, each a segment cut off by a 60° chord. Find the cost of making them at ₹0.35 per cm². (π = 22/7, √3 = 1.7)
question_hinglish: 28 cm radius ke gol table cover pe chhe barabar designs hain, har ek 60° chord se kata segment. ₹0.35 prati cm² ki dar se banaane ki laagat nikaalo. (π = 22/7, √3 = 1.7)
answer_english:
Each 60° sector = (1/6) × (22/7) × 784 = 1232/3 ≈ 410.67 cm².
Each equilateral triangle (side 28) = (1.7/4) × 784 = 333.2 cm².
One segment ≈ 410.67 − 333.2 = 77.47 cm²; six segments ≈ 464.8 cm².
Cost ≈ 464.8 × 0.35 ≈ ₹162.68.

question_english: Differentiate between a sector and a segment of a circle. How are their areas related?
question_hinglish: Circle ke sector aur segment mein antar batao. Unke area kaise jude hain?
answer_english:
Sector: bounded by two radii and an arc, like a slice of pizza. Area = (θ/360)πr².
Segment: bounded by a chord and an arc, the region cut off by a chord. It has no radii as boundaries.
Relation: area of segment = area of the sector with the same arc − area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.
answer_hinglish:
Sector: do radii aur ek arc se ghira, pizza ke tukde jaisa. Area = (θ/360)πr².
Segment: ek chord aur arc se ghira, chord se kata hissa. Iski seema mein radii nahi hote.
Sambandh: segment ka area = same arc waale sector ka area − do radii aur chord se bane triangle ka area.
ncert_context: Recall that the portion (or part) of the circular region enclosed by two radii and the corresponding arc is called a sector of the circle and the portion (or part) of the circular region enclosed between a chord and the corresponding arc is called a segment of the circle. Area of the sector of angle θ = (θ/360) × πr². Area of the segment APB = Area of the sector OAPB – Area of Δ OAB. Area of segment of a circle = Area of the corresponding sector – Area of the corresponding triangle.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: How do we find the surface area of a solid made by combining basic solids? Why is it not the sum of the total surface areas of the parts?
question_hinglish: Basic solids ko jodkar bane solid ka surface area kaise nikaalte hain? Ye hisson ke total surface areas ka jod kyun nahi hota?
answer_english:
Break the solid into basic solids we already know (cuboid, cone, cylinder, sphere, hemisphere) and add only the surfaces that remain visible.
Example: an oil-tanker container is a cylinder with two hemispherical ends, so TSA = CSA of hemisphere + CSA of cylinder + CSA of other hemisphere.
A round-bottomed toy (cone on a hemisphere) has TSA = CSA of hemisphere + CSA of cone.
It is not the sum of the parts' total surface areas, because the faces that are joined together (like the flat bases) disappear inside the new solid.
answer_hinglish:
Solid ko jaane-pehchaane basic solids (cuboid, cone, cylinder, sphere, hemisphere) mein todo aur sirf bahar dikhne waali satahein jodo.
Udaharan: oil tanker ka container cylinder aur do hemispherical siron se bana hai, toh TSA = hemisphere ka CSA + cylinder ka CSA + doosre hemisphere ka CSA.
Gol tale waala khilona (hemisphere pe cone) ka TSA = hemisphere ka CSA + cone ka CSA.
Ye hisson ke TSA ka jod nahi hota, kyunki jo satahein judti hain (jaise chapte base) woh naye solid ke andar chhup jaati hain.
ncert_context: Now, whenever we come across a new problem, we first try to see, if we can break it down into smaller problems, we have earlier solved. We can see that this solid is made up of a cylinder with two hemispheres stuck at either end. If we consider the surface of the newly formed object, we would be able to see only the curved surfaces of the two hemispheres and the curved surface of the cylinder. So, the total surface area of the new solid is the sum of the curved surface areas of each of the individual parts. This gives, TSA of new solid = CSA of one hemisphere + CSA of cylinder + CSA of other hemisphere. Total surface area of the toy = CSA of hemisphere + CSA of cone. You may note that 'total surface area of the top' is not the sum of the total surface areas of the cone and hemisphere.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: How does finding the volume of a combined solid differ from finding its surface area?
question_hinglish: Jode hue solid ka volume nikaalna uska surface area nikaalne se kaise alag hai?
answer_english:
Surface area: we cannot simply add the parts' surface areas, because the joined faces disappear. Only the exposed surfaces are added.
Volume: no volume is lost when solids are joined, so the volume of the combined solid is the sum of the volumes of its parts.
When a part is removed (a cavity or depression), its volume is subtracted.
answer_hinglish:
Surface area: hisson ke surface areas seedhe nahi jod sakte, kyunki judi hui satahein gaayab ho jaati hain. Sirf bahar ki satahein judti hain.
Volume: solids jodne pe koi volume kam nahi hota, toh jode hue solid ka volume hisson ke volumes ka jod hai.
Jab koi hissa nikaala jaaye (cavity ya depression), uska volume ghataaya jaata hai.
ncert_context: It may be noted that in calculating the surface area, we have not added the surface areas of the two constituents, because some part of the surface area disappeared in the process of joining them. However, this will not be the case when we calculate the volume. The volume of the solid formed by joining two basic solids will actually be the sum of the volumes of the constituents. But the actual capacity of the glass is less by the volume of the hemisphere at the base of the glass.

Answer the question in English using only the given context.

Surface area: we cannot simply add the parts' surface areas, because the joined faces disappear. Only the exposed surfaces are added.
Volume: no volume is lost when solids are joined, so the volume of the combined solid is the sum of the volumes of its parts.
When a part is removed (a cavity or depression), its volume is subtracted.

question_english: (a) A decorative block is a 5 cm cube with a hemisphere of diameter 4.2 cm on top. Find its total surface area. (b) A cubical block of side 7 cm is surmounted by a hemisphere. What is the greatest possible diameter of the hemisphere, and what is the surface area? (π = 22/7)
question_hinglish: (a) Ek decorative block 5 cm ka cube hai jiske upar 4.2 cm diameter ka hemisphere hai. Iska total surface area nikaalo. (b) 7 cm side ke cube pe hemisphere laga hai. Hemisphere ka sabse bada sambhav diameter kya hai, aur surface area kitna hai? (π = 22/7)
answer_english:
(a) SA = TSA of cube − base of hemisphere + CSA of hemisphere = 150 − πr² + 2πr² = 150 + πr² = 150 + (22/7)(2.1)² = 150 + 13.86 = 163.86 cm².
(b) The greatest diameter equals the side, 7 cm (r = 3.5).
SA = 6 × 49 + πr² = 294 + (22/7)(12.25) = 294 + 38.5 = 332.5 cm².
