question_english: A toy rocket is a cone on a cylinder: total height 26 cm, cone height 6 cm, cone base diameter 5 cm, cylinder diameter 3 cm. The cone is painted orange and the cylinder yellow. Find each area. (π = 3.14)
question_hinglish: Khilona rocket cylinder pe cone hai: kul oonchai 26 cm, cone ki oonchai 6 cm, cone ke base ka diameter 5 cm, cylinder ka diameter 3 cm. Cone orange aur cylinder yellow rangna hai. Dono area nikaalo. (π = 3.14)
answer_english:
Cone: r = 2.5, h = 6, l = √(6.25 + 36) = 6.5 cm. Cylinder: r′ = 1.5, h′ = 20 cm.
The cone's base is wider than the cylinder, so a ring of the cone's base is also exposed.
Orange = πrl + πr² − πr′² = π(16.25 + 6.25 − 2.25) = 3.14 × 20.25 = 63.585 cm².
Yellow = CSA of cylinder + one base = πr′(2h′ + r′) = 3.14 × 1.5 × 41.5 = 195.465 cm².
answer_hinglish:
Cone: r = 2.5, h = 6, l = √(6.25 + 36) = 6.5 cm. Cylinder: r′ = 1.5, h′ = 20 cm.
Cone ka base cylinder se chauda hai, toh cone ke base ki ek ring bhi bahar dikhti hai.
Orange = πrl + πr² − πr′² = π(16.25 + 6.25 − 2.25) = 3.14 × 20.25 = 63.585 cm².
Yellow = cylinder ka CSA + ek base = πr′(2h′ + r′) = 3.14 × 1.5 × 41.5 = 195.465 cm².
ncert_context: Example 3: A wooden toy rocket is in the shape of a cone mounted on a cylinder. The height of the entire rocket is 26 cm, while the height of the conical part is 6 cm. The base of the conical portion has a diameter of 5 cm, while the base diameter of the cylindrical portion is 3 cm. If the conical portion is to be painted orange and the cylindrical portion yellow, find the area of the rocket painted with each of these colours. (Take π = 3.14) r = 2.5 cm, h = 6 cm, r′ = 1.5 cm, h′ = 26 – 6 = 20 cm and l = 6.5 cm. The base of the cone is larger than the base of the cylinder. So, a part of the base of the cone (a ring) is to be painted. The area to be painted orange = CSA of the cone + base area of the cone – base area of the cylinder = π[(2.5 × 6.5) + (2.5)² – (1.5)²] = 63.585 cm². The area to be painted yellow = CSA of the cylinder + area of one base of the cylinder = πr′(2h′ + r′) = 195.465 cm².

question_hinglish: (a) Mayank ka bird-bath 1.45 m ooncha, 30 cm radius ka cylinder hai jiske ek sire pe hemispherical gaddha hai. Iska total surface area nikaalo. (b) 64 cm³ ke do cubes sire se sira jode gaye. Cuboid ka surface area nikaalo. (π = 22/7)

SA = 2(8×4 + 4×4 + 8×4) = 2(32 + 16 + 32) = 160 cm².

question_english: Shanta's shed is a cuboid (base 7 m × 15 m, height 8 m) surmounted by a half cylinder. Find the volume of air it holds. Machinery takes 300 m³ and 20 workers take 0.08 m³ each. How much air remains? (π = 22/7)
question_hinglish: Shanta ka shed cuboid (base 7 m × 15 m, oonchai 8 m) hai jiske upar aadha cylinder hai. Usme kitni hawa samaati hai? Machinery 300 m³ aur 20 mazdoor 0.08 m³ har ek lete hain. Kitni hawa bachti hai? (π = 22/7)
ncert_context: Example 5: Shanta runs an industry in a shed which is in the shape of a cuboid surmounted by a half cylinder. If the base of the shed is of dimension 7 m × 15 m, and the height of the cuboidal portion is 8 m, find the volume of air that the shed can hold. Further, suppose the machinery in the shed occupies a total space of 300 m³, and there are 20 workers, each of whom occupy about 0.08 m³ space on an average. Then, how much air is in the shed? The required volume = volume of the cuboid + ½ volume of the cylinder = 1128.75 m³. The total space occupied by the machinery = 300 m³. The total space occupied by the workers = 20 × 0.08 m³ = 1.6 m³. Therefore, the volume of the air = 1128.75 – (300.00 + 1.60) = 827.15 m³.

Sphere: r = 4.25 cm, V = (4/3) × 3.14 × 4.25³ = (4/3) × 3.14 × 76.765625 ≈ 321.39 cm³.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: How is the mean of grouped data found? What is a class mark, and why does the grouped mean differ slightly from the exact mean?
question_hinglish: Grouped data ka mean kaise nikaalte hain? Class mark kya hai, aur grouped mean asli mean se thoda alag kyun aata hai?
answer_english:
For observations x₁, …, xₙ with frequencies f₁, …, fₙ: mean x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ.
For grouped data, each class is represented by its class mark (mid-point) = (upper limit + lower limit)/2, assuming the frequency is centred there. Using class marks as xᵢ is the Direct Method.
Example: the ungrouped marks of 30 students give an exact mean of 1779/30 = 59.3. Grouping them into classes of width 15 gives Σfᵢxᵢ = 1860 and mean 62.
The difference comes from the mid-point assumption: 59.3 is exact, while 62 is approximate.
answer_hinglish:
Observations x₁, …, xₙ aur frequencies f₁, …, fₙ ke liye: mean x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ.
Grouped data mein har class ko uske class mark (mid-point) = (upper limit + lower limit)/2 se dikhaate hain, ye maankar ki frequency wahin kendrit hai. Class marks ko xᵢ lena Direct Method hai.
Udaharan: 30 students ke ungrouped marks ka asli mean 1779/30 = 59.3 hai. 15 chaudai ki classes mein group karne pe Σfᵢxᵢ = 1860 aur mean 62 aata hai.
Ye fark mid-point maanyata se hai: 59.3 sateek hai, jabki 62 approximate.
ncert_context: If x₁, x₂, . . ., xₙ are observations with respective frequencies f₁, f₂, . . ., fₙ, then the sum of the values of all the observations = f₁x₁ + f₂x₂ + . . . + fₙxₙ, and the number of observations = f₁ + f₂ + . . . + fₙ. So, the mean x̄ of the data is given by x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ. The mean marks obtained is 59.3. It is assumed that the frequency of each class-interval is centred around its mid-point. So the mid-point (or class mark) of each class can be chosen to represent the observations falling in the class. Class mark = (Upper class limit + Lower class limit)/2. The mean x̄ of the given data is given by x̄ = 1860.0/30 = 62. This new method of finding the mean is known as the Direct Method. The difference in the two values is because of the mid-point assumption, 59.3 being the exact mean, while 62 an approximate mean.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Compare the direct, assumed mean and step-deviation methods for finding the mean of grouped data. When is each convenient?
question_hinglish: Grouped data ka mean nikaalne ke direct, assumed mean aur step-deviation methods ki tulna karo. Har ek kab suvidhajanak hai?
answer_english:
Direct: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ. Best when xᵢ and fᵢ are small.
Assumed mean: choose a central xᵢ as a and set dᵢ = xᵢ − a; then x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ/Σfᵢ. Reduces large products.
Step-deviation: uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h with h the class size (or a common factor of all dᵢ); then x̄ = a + h × Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ. Most convenient when all dᵢ share a common factor; it also works for unequal class sizes with a suitable h.
All three give the same mean, and the result does not depend on the choice of a. The last two are just simplified forms of the direct method.
answer_hinglish:
Direct: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ. Jab xᵢ aur fᵢ chhote hon tab best.
Assumed mean: beech ka koi xᵢ a chuno aur dᵢ = xᵢ − a lo; tab x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ/Σfᵢ. Bade guna kam ho jaate hain.
Step-deviation: uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h jahan h class size (ya saare dᵢ ka common factor) hai; tab x̄ = a + h × Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ. Jab saare dᵢ ka common factor ho tab sabse aasaan; unequal class sizes mein bhi sahi h lekar chalta hai.
Teenon same mean dete hain, aur jawab a ke chunaav pe nirbhar nahi karta. Aakhri do direct method ke hi saral roop hain.
ncert_context: The first step is to choose one among the xᵢ's as the assumed mean, and denote it by 'a'. The next step is to find the difference dᵢ between a and each of the xᵢ's. x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ/Σfᵢ. The method discussed above is called the Assumed Mean Method. So, we can say that the value of the mean obtained does not depend on the choice of 'a'. Let uᵢ = (xᵢ – a)/h, where a is the assumed mean and h is the class size. x̄ = a + h(Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ). The method discussed above is called the Step-deviation method. The step-deviation method will be convenient to apply if all the dᵢ's have a common factor. The mean obtained by all the three methods is the same. The assumed mean method and step-deviation method are just simplified forms of the direct method. If xᵢ and fᵢ are sufficiently small, then the direct method is an appropriate choice. If the class sizes are unequal, and xᵢ are large numerically, we can still apply the step-deviation method by taking h to be a suitable divisor of all the dᵢ's.

Compare the direct, assumed mean and step-deviation methods for finding the mean of grouped data. When is each convenient?

Step-deviation: uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h with h the class size (or a common factor of all dᵢ); then x̄ = a + h × Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ. Most convenient when all dᵢ share a common factor; it also works for unequal class sizes with a suitable h.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: What is the modal class? State the formula for the mode of grouped data.
question_hinglish: Modal class kya hai? Grouped data ke mode ka formula batao.
answer_english:
In grouped data the mode cannot be read off the frequencies. We can only locate the modal class, the class with the maximum frequency. The mode is a value inside it:
Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h
where l = lower limit of the modal class, h = class size, f₁ = frequency of the modal class, f₀ = frequency of the preceding class, f₂ = frequency of the succeeding class.
Data with more than one maximum-frequency value is multimodal. The class intervals must be continuous before applying the formula.

jahan l = modal class ki lower limit, h = class size, f₁ = modal class ki frequency, f₀ = pichhli class ki frequency, f₂ = agli class ki frequency.
Jisme ek se zyada values ki sabse zyada frequency ho, woh data multimodal hai. Formula lagaane se pehle class intervals continuous hone chahiye.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: What is cumulative frequency? Distinguish between 'less than' and 'more than' cumulative frequency distributions.
question_hinglish: Cumulative frequency kya hai? 'Less than' aur 'more than' cumulative frequency distributions mein antar batao.
answer_english:
The cumulative frequency of a class is the sum of the frequencies of all classes up to and including it.
Less than type: counts observations below each upper limit, e.g. less than 10: 5, less than 20: 5 + 3 = 8, …, less than 100: 53. The upper limits are used.
More than type: counts observations greater than or equal to each lower limit, e.g. ≥ 0: 53, ≥ 10: 53 − 5 = 48, ≥ 20: 45, …. The lower limits are used.
Either can be used to find the median.
answer_hinglish:
Kisi class ki cumulative frequency, us class tak (use milaakar) saari classes ki frequencies ka jod hai.
Less than type: har upper limit se kam observations ginta hai, jaise 10 se kam: 5, 20 se kam: 5 + 3 = 8, …, 100 se kam: 53. Upper limits use hoti hain.
More than type: har lower limit ke barabar ya zyada observations ginta hai, jaise ≥ 0: 53, ≥ 10: 53 − 5 = 48, ≥ 20: 45, …. Lower limits use hoti hain.
Median nikaalne ke liye dono mein se koi bhi use kar sakte hain.
ncert_context: The cumulative frequency of a class is the frequency obtained by adding the frequencies of all the classes preceding the given class. How many students have scored less than 20 marks? The total number of students with marks less than 20 is 5 + 3, i.e., 8. We say that the cumulative frequency of the class 10-20 is 8. The distribution given above is called the cumulative frequency distribution of the less than type. Here 10, 20, 30, . . . 100, are the upper limits of the respective class intervals. All 53 students have scored marks more than or equal to 0. There are 53 – 5 = 48 students getting more than or equal to 10 marks. The table above is called a cumulative frequency distribution of the more than type. Here 0, 10, 20, . . ., 90 give the lower limits of the respective class intervals. Now, to find the median of grouped data, we can make use of any of these cumulative frequency distributions.

question_english: How is the median of ungrouped and grouped data found? State the median formula.
question_hinglish: Ungrouped aur grouped data ka median kaise nikaalte hain? Median ka formula batao.
answer_english:
Ungrouped: arrange the data in order. If n is odd, the median is the ((n + 1)/2)th observation. If n is even, it is the average of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th observations. E.g. for 100 students it is the average of the 50th (28) and 51st (29) values = 28.5.
Grouped: find the cumulative frequencies and n/2. The median class is the class whose cumulative frequency is greater than and nearest to n/2.

About half the observations lie below the median and half above.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: When should the mean, median or mode be used? State the empirical relationship between them.
question_hinglish: Mean, median ya mode kab use karna chahiye? Inke beech ka empirical sambandh batao.
answer_english:
Mean: the most used measure. It uses all observations, lies between the extremes and allows comparison of distributions (e.g. comparing schools' average results). But extreme values distort it.
Median: better when a 'typical' value is wanted and extreme values exist, e.g. typical productivity of workers or average wage in a country.
Mode: best for the most frequent or popular item, e.g. the most watched TV programme, the consumer item in greatest demand, or the most common vehicle colour.
Empirical relationship: 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean.
answer_hinglish:
Mean: sabse zyada use hone waala maap. Ye saare observations leta hai, extremes ke beech hota hai aur distributions ki tulna karne deta hai (jaise schoolon ke ausat result). Par extreme values ise bigaad deti hain.
Median: jab 'typical' value chahiye aur extreme values hon tab behtar, jaise mazdooron ki typical productivity ya desh ki ausat mazdoori.
Mode: sabse zyada baar aane waali ya lokpriya cheez ke liye best, jaise sabse zyada dekha jaane waala TV programme, sabse zyada maang waali cheez, ya gaadiyon ka sabse aam rang.
Empirical sambandh: 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean.

In problems where individual observations are not important, and we wish to find out a 'typical' observation, the median is more appropriate, e.g., finding the typical productivity rate of workers, average wage in a country, etc. In situations which require establishing the most frequent value or most popular item, the mode is the best choice, e.g., to find the most popular T.V. programme being watched, the consumer item in greatest demand, the colour of the vehicle used by most of the people, etc. Remarks: 1. question_english: Define the theoretical (classical) probability of an event. Who gave this definition?
question_hinglish: Kisi event ki theoretical (classical) probability define karo. Ye definition kisne di?
answer_english:
P(E) = (number of outcomes favourable to E) / (number of all possible outcomes of the experiment), assuming the outcomes are equally likely.
This definition was given by Pierre Simon Laplace in 1795.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Compare experimental (empirical) and theoretical probability. Why is theoretical probability needed?
question_hinglish: Experimental (empirical) aur theoretical probability ki tulna karo. Theoretical probability ki zaroorat kyun hai?
answer_english:
Experimental: P(E) = (number of trials in which E happened)/(total number of trials). It is based on what actually happened and needs the experiment to be repeated many times.
Theoretical: P(E) = favourable outcomes/all possible outcomes, assuming equally likely outcomes. It predicts what will happen.
Repeating some experiments is very expensive or impossible, like launching satellites or waiting for earthquakes, so the equally-likely assumption lets us compute the exact probability directly.
As the number of trials increases, the experimental and theoretical probabilities come close.

Theoretical: P(E) = anukool outcomes/saare sambhav outcomes, equally likely maankar. Ye bataati hai ki kya hoga.
Kuch experiments dohraana bahut mehenga ya asambhav hai, jaise satellite launch karna ya bhookamp ka intezaar, toh equally-likely maanyata se sateek probability seedhe nikal jaati hai.
Trials badhne pe experimental aur theoretical probability paas aa jaati hain.

But how about repeating the experiment of launching a satellite in order to compute the empirical probability of its failure during launching, or the repetition of the phenomenon of an earthquake? The experimental or empirical probability of an event is based on what has actually happened while the theoretical probability of the event attempts to predict what will happen on the basis of certain assumptions. As the number of trials in an experiment, go on increasing we may expect the experimental and theoretical probabilities to be nearly the same.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: What are equally likely outcomes? Give examples and a non-example.
question_hinglish: Equally likely outcomes kya hote hain? Udaharan aur ek ulta udaharan do.
answer_english:
Outcomes are equally likely when each has the same chance of occurring.
Examples: tossing a fair (unbiased) coin gives head or tail equally likely. A fair die gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 equally likely.
Non-example: a bag with 4 red balls and 1 blue ball. Red is more likely than blue, so 'red' and 'blue' are not equally likely, although drawing any particular ball is equally likely.
So not all experiments have equally likely outcomes.

Ulta udaharan: 4 laal aur 1 neeli gend waala thaila. Laal ka mauka neeli se zyada hai, toh 'laal' aur 'neeli' equally likely nahi, haalaanki koi ek khaas gend nikalna equally likely hai.
Toh har experiment ke outcomes equally likely nahi hote.
ncert_context: When we speak of a coin, we assume it to be 'fair', that is, it is symmetrical so that there is no reason for it to come down more often on one side than the other. We call this property of the coin as being 'unbiased'. We can reasonably assume that each outcome, head or tail, is as likely to occur as the other. We refer to this by saying that the outcomes head and tail, are equally likely. Suppose we throw a die once. The equally likely outcomes of throwing a die are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Suppose that a bag contains 4 red balls and 1 blue ball. Since there are 4 red balls and only one blue ball, you would agree that you are more likely to get a red ball than a blue ball. So, the outcomes (a red ball or a blue ball) are not equally likely. However, the outcome of drawing a ball of any colour from the bag is equally likely. So, all experiments do not necessarily have equally likely outcomes.

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Explain elementary events, complementary events, sure events and impossible events, with the range of probability.
question_hinglish: Elementary events, complementary events, sure events aur impossible events samjhaao, probability ki range ke saath.
answer_english:
Elementary event: an event with only one outcome (e.g. getting a head). The probabilities of all elementary events of an experiment add up to 1.
Complementary events: E and 'not E' (Ē). P(E) + P(Ē) = 1, so P(Ē) = 1 − P(E).
Impossible event: cannot happen, P = 0 (e.g. getting 8 on a die).
Sure (certain) event: always happens, P = 1 (e.g. getting a number less than 7 on a die).
Since favourable outcomes ≤ all outcomes, 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.
answer_hinglish:
Elementary event: sirf ek outcome waala event (jaise head aana). Experiment ke saare elementary events ki probabilities ka jod 1 hota hai.
Complementary events: E aur 'not E' (Ē). P(E) + P(Ē) = 1, toh P(Ē) = 1 − P(E).
Impossible event: ho hi nahi sakta, P = 0 (jaise die pe 8 aana).
Sure (certain) event: hamesha hota hai, P = 1 (jaise die pe 7 se kam number aana).
Anukool outcomes ≤ saare outcomes, isliye 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.
ncert_context: An event having only one outcome of the experiment is called an elementary event. Observe that the sum of the probabilities of all the elementary events of an experiment is 1. We denote the event 'not E' by Ē. So, P(E) + P(not E) = 1, which gives us P(Ē) = 1 – P(E). The event Ē, representing 'not E', is called the complement of the event E. We also say that E and Ē are complementary events. Getting 8 in a single throw of a die, is impossible. So, P(getting 8) = 0/6 = 0. That is, the probability of an event which is impossible to occur is 0. Such an event is called an impossible event. P(getting a number less than 7) = 6/6 = 1. So, the probability of an event which is sure (or certain) to occur is 1. Such an event is called a sure event or a certain event. The numerator is always less than or equal to the denominator. Therefore, 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.

That is, the probability of an event which is impossible to occur is 0. Such an event is called an impossible event. P(getting a number less than 7) = 6/6 = 1. So, the probability of an event which is sure (or certain) to occur is 1. Such an event is called a sure event or a certain event. The numerator is always less than or equal to the denominator. Therefore, 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.

Question:
Elementary events, complementary events, sure events aur impossible events samjhaao, probability ki range ke saath.

Sure (certain) event: hamesha hota hai, P = 1 (jaise die pe 7 se kam number aana).

question_english: Briefly describe the history of probability theory.
question_hinglish: Probability theory ka itihaas sankshep mein batao.
answer_english:
Probability theory began in the 16th century when the Italian physician and mathematician J. Cardan wrote the first book on it, 'The Book on Games of Chance'.
James Bernoulli (1654–1705), A. de Moivre (1667–1754) and Pierre Simon Laplace made major contributions. Laplace's 'Théorie Analytique des Probabilités' (1812) is considered the greatest single contribution.
Today probability is used in biology, economics, genetics, physics, sociology and more.

question_english: (a) Find P(head) and P(tail) for one coin toss. (b) Kritika draws one ball from a bag with one red, one blue and one yellow ball. Find each probability. (c) A die is thrown once: find P(number > 4) and P(number ≤ 4).
question_hinglish: (a) Ek baar sikka uchhaalne pe P(head) aur P(tail) nikaalo. (b) Kritika ek laal, ek neeli aur ek peeli gend waale thaile se ek gend nikaalti hai. Har probability nikaalo. (c) Die ek baar phenkne pe P(number > 4) aur P(number ≤ 4) nikaalo.
answer_english:
(a) Outcomes: H, T. P(head) = 1/2, P(tail) = 1/2.
(b) 3 equally likely outcomes: P(yellow) = P(red) = P(blue) = 1/3. These are elementary events, and their sum is 1.
(c) P(> 4) = P(5 or 6) = 2/6 = 1/3. P(≤ 4) = 4/6 = 2/3. These events are complementary: 1/3 + 2/3 = 1.

question_english: (a) One card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52. Find P(ace) and P(not an ace). (b) Sangeeta's probability of winning a tennis match against Reshma is 0.62. Find Reshma's probability of winning.
question_hinglish: (a) 52 ke achchhe se phente deck se ek card nikaala. P(ikka) aur P(ikka nahi) nikaalo. (b) Sangeeta ke Reshma se tennis match jeetne ki probability 0.62 hai. Reshma ke jeetne ki probability nikaalo.
answer_english:
(a) There are 4 aces: P(ace) = 4/52 = 1/13. P(not ace) = 48/52 = 12/13, or 1 − 1/13 = 12/13.
(b) The events are complementary: P(Reshma) = 1 − 0.62 = 0.38.

question_english: (a) Savita and Hamida are friends. Ignoring leap years, find P(different birthdays) and P(same birthday). (b) In a group of 3 students, P(2 students do not share a birthday) = 0.992. Find P(they share a birthday).
question_hinglish: (a) Savita aur Hamida dost hain. Leap year chhodkar P(alag birthdays) aur P(same birthday) nikaalo. (b) 3 students ke group mein P(2 students ka birthday same nahi) = 0.992. P(unka birthday same) nikaalo.
answer_english:
(a) Hamida's birthday can be any of 365 days. Different from Savita's: 364 favourable → P = 364/365.
Same birthday = 1 − 364/365 = 1/365.
(b) Complementary: 1 − 0.992 = 0.008.
answer_hinglish:
(a) Hamida ka birthday 365 mein se koi bhi din ho sakta hai. Savita se alag: 364 anukool → P = 364/365.
Same birthday = 1 − 364/365 = 1/365.
(b) Complementary: 1 − 0.992 = 0.008.

question_english: (a) Harpreet tosses two different coins together. Find P(at least one head). (b) Hanif tosses a coin 3 times and wins only if all results are the same. Find P(Hanif loses).

question_english: A die is thrown twice. Find P(5 does not come up either time) and P(5 comes up at least once).

subject: Mathematics
question_english: Which arguments are correct? (i) Two coins have three outcomes (two heads, two tails, one of each), so each has probability 1/3. (ii) A die gives odd or even, so P(odd) = 1/2. (iii) Two dice give sums 2 to 12, eleven outcomes, so each sum has probability 1/11.
question_hinglish: Kaun se tark sahi hain? (i) Do sikkon ke teen outcomes (do head, do tail, ek-ek) hain, toh har ek ki probability 1/3. (ii) Die pe odd ya even aata hai, toh P(odd) = 1/2. (iii) Do dice ke jod 2 se 12, gyaarah outcomes, toh har jod ki probability 1/11.
answer_english:
(i) Incorrect: the three outcomes are not equally likely. The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT, so P(two heads) = 1/4, P(two tails) = 1/4, P(one of each) = 2/4 = 1/2.
(ii) Correct: 3 odd (1, 3, 5) out of 6 equally likely faces gives 3/6 = 1/2.
(iii) Incorrect: the sums are not equally likely. Sum 7 has 6 ways (6/36) while sum 2 has only 1 (1/36).
Lesson: the classical formula applies only to equally likely outcomes.

(ii) Sahi: 6 equally likely faces mein 3 odd (1, 3, 5), toh 3/6 = 1/2.
(iii) Galat: jod equally likely nahi hain. Jod 7 ke 6 tareeke hain (6/36) jabki jod 2 ka sirf 1 (1/36).
Seekh: classical formula sirf equally likely outcomes pe lagta hai.
